docs.title: OpenEnergy
docs.text:
OpenEnergy backtests battery storage and renewable plants against real day-ahead power prices. You describe the assets and a forecasting approach in a short YAML file; OpenEnergy plans each day on the forecast, settles the plan at the prices that actually cleared, and tells you what the site earned, how hard the battery worked, and how close it came to a perfect-foresight benchmark.

It is built for research questions such as:

  • How much is a 2-hour battery worth in the GB day-ahead market?
  • How much more does it earn selling frequency response too?
  • How much revenue does a better price forecast buy?
  • How much of the average price do solar and wind actually capture?
  • Can a battery share a solar farm's grid connection without losing money?
  • As wind and solar grow, how much surplus appears, and how much storage absorbs it?
  • What do storage and renewables do to emissions, and what does a carbon price change?
  • How well does a cost-based model of GB plants reproduce real prices, and what changes with more wind, more storage or a different carbon price?
  • What might GB prices and a battery look like on NESO's Future Energy Scenarios, with interconnectors trading at neighbouring markets' prices?

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/koulakhilesh/OpenEnergy.git
cd OpenEnergy
uv sync --extra forecast
uv run openenergy compare examples/gb-2019-{naive,ml,perfect}.yaml

scenario         forecast             days       revenue   per MW-yr   capture   cycles
gb-2019-perfect  perfect_foresight     363        19,075      19,180    100.0%      464
gb-2019-ml       gradient_boosting     363        14,086      14,164     73.8%      400
gb-2019-naive    naive_last_week       363        13,920      13,996     73.0%      465

A 1 MW / 2 MWh battery trading GB day-ahead prices in 2019 would have earned about £14k per MW-year planning on last week's prices, or 73% of what perfect foresight allows.

The same battery on every year of the bundled prices (examples/gb-2022-naive.yaml with other dates, and with forecast: {method: fundamentals, path: ...}; Ember prices, GBP per MW-year):

Year 2017 2018 2019 2020 2021 2022 2023 2024 2025 Last week's prices 20,633 18,887 13,943 17,144 74,169 76,948 35,957 28,690 35,861 OpenEnergy forecast 15,148 18,382 70,771 80,150 39,415 33,410 39,361 Perfect foresight 26,252 25,380 19,538 22,362 89,282 102,550 45,968 38,870 44,564 Capture, last week's prices 79% 74% 71% 77% 83% 75% 78% 74% 80% Capture, OpenEnergy forecast 78% 82% 79% 78% 86% 86% 88%

Revenue followed the gas crisis: over five times the 2019 level in 2021–2022, and 2.1 to 2.6 times it in 2023–2025. Last week's prices kept 71–83% of the perfect-foresight value every year; OpenEnergy's forecast (NESO's demand forecast, Elexon's wind forecast, the daily gas price and recent prices, as known the day before) kept 78–88% and did better every year except 2021, when gas prices rose faster than a model trained on calmer years could follow (see Research).

Renewables are one command away:

uv run openenergy capture data/time_series/time_series_60min_singleindex_filtered.csv -t solar

GB solar captured 94–106% of the average day-ahead price each year from 2015 to 2019, and adding a 5 MW battery behind an existing 10 MW solar connection cost almost nothing in lost trading (see Research).

The whole system is one command too:

uv run openenergy netload data/time_series/time_series_60min_singleindex_filtered.csv \
  --scale-wind 3 --scale-solar 3 --must-run 8000

Tripling 2019 wind and solar would leave 14 TWh of surplus above an 8 GW must-run floor; a 10 GW / 24 h storage fleet absorbs about three-quarters of it (see System analysis).

And the plants behind the price:

uv run openenergy system validate

Rebuilt from fuel, carbon and fleet data alone, GB's 2019 average price comes out at £38.1/MWh against £42.9 actual, with a correlation of 0.69, but its peaks are far too low: a battery that earned £16k per MW-year on real 2019 prices earns almost nothing on the modelled ones. With the daily gas price (v6.0), the model follows the 2022 gas crisis with a correlation of 0.81 (0.40 with quarterly prices) (see System model).

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
1. Loads prices, capacity factors, demand and carbon intensity from the bundled Open Power System Data, Ember and NESO extracts (GB prices to October 2026) and checks them: UTC timestamps, a regular grid, reported gaps and filtered telemetry glitches.
  2. Forecasts each day using only data available at the decision time (noon the day before by default), from last week's prices to OpenEnergy's forecast built on NESO's demand and Elexon's wind forecasts and the daily gas price.
  3. Plans the day with a mixed-integer optimisation that respects power and energy limits, efficiencies, an end-of-day state of charge and, for co-located sites, a shared grid connection; an optional carbon price steers dispatch.
  4. Settles the plan at actual prices through the battery physics, including cycle and calendar ageing.
  5. Reports revenue, cycles, state of health, forecast error, the capture ratio against perfect foresight, net emissions and, for sites, curtailment, the plant's captured price and the value of co-location against separate connections.
  6. Analyses the system: net load, ramps and surplus as renewables scale, and the storage needed to absorb that surplus; openenergy sweep sizes storage for a site.
  7. Models GB dispatch: CCGT, coal and peaking plant in merit order from DUKES fleet data, fuel and carbon prices, checked against 2015–2025, with scenarios for renewables, storage, fleet and carbon policy (storage via the optional PyPSA backend), and optional unit commitment with start-up costs and minimum stable output.
  8. Reports any saved run, system scenario, backcast or sweep as one interactive HTML page of charts and tables (openenergy report; see the example).
  9. Stacks revenue: GB Dynamic Containment, Moderation and Regulation co-optimised with day-ahead trading in the same plan, with the energy each service moves taken from GB frequency data (see Revenue stacking).
  10. Looks forward: NESO Future Energy Scenarios pathways to 2035 on a historic weather year, made secure to GB's reliability standard, with GB's interconnectors as price-taking links to six neighbouring markets at availabilities fitted from their actual flows, and unit commitment; and how much storage GB can use before a battery stops paying (see Forward scenarios).
  11. Runs in the browser: a web app simulates Britain's grid hour by hour from 2019, with a battery trading on a plan the optimiser makes in your browser, lets you play a day against it, and values a battery on any GB year from 2017 or on a FES pathway; try it at open-energy-eight.vercel.app.
  12. Checks itself against real batteries: every GB grid battery's metered output and Balancing Mechanism cashflows from Elexon since 2021, next to what the optimiser does, north and south of the Scottish border (see Real batteries).

See Concepts for the equations and Scenarios for every setting.

docs.title: Roadmap
docs.text:
Released

Release Scope v2.0 Battery arbitrage backtesting: physics, ageing, dispatch, forecasters, CLI v2.1 PV and wind assets, captured price, co-located storage v2.2 Net load, surplus, storage sizing, emissions v3.0 GB system dispatch with conventional generation via PyPSA, checked against 2015–2020 v3.1 Optional unit commitment (start-up costs, minimum stable output) and a start-cost price, re-checked against 2015–2020 without fitting to prices v3.2 Data to 2025: GB prices from Ember, NESO generation and carbon intensity, DUKES and fuel prices, UK ETS; openenergy data update; backcast of the gas crisis and coal exit v3.3 Multi-day planning horizon (dispatch.lookahead_days), and a measured answer on planning under price uncertainty: for day-ahead-only trading a scenario plan equals one forecast, and risk aversion costs revenue v3.4 Reports: openenergy report turns saved runs, system scenarios, backcasts and sweeps into one interactive HTML file; chart functions reusable from Python v3.5 Revenue stacking: GB Dynamic Containment, Moderation and Regulation co-optimised with day-ahead trading; a measured answer on balancing (imbalance prices are valuable only with a forecast open data does not give; revised in v6.0) and on stochastic planning (still no value) v4.0 Forward scenarios from NESO's Future Energy Scenarios on a historic weather year; GB's interconnectors as price-taking links to six neighbouring markets, checked against actual flows 2019–2025; a web app (FastAPI, Vercel) valuing a battery on history or a FES pathway v4.1 A usable web app: the answer first in plain words, instant results for common batteries, value by year and by FES pathway at a glance, side-by-side comparison with shareable links, explanations next to each term, CSV and scenario downloads, and a JSON API; CITATION.cff and PyPI release v4.2 A more credible model: unit commitment with interconnector links; each link's availability fitted from its actual flows, never from prices; a measured answer on the missing daily spread (the everyday intraday shape, not negative prices); forward scenarios and the app re-run. GB zones were dropped: GB keeps one national wholesale price (DESNZ, REMA summer update, July 2025) v5.0 A React and TypeScript front end on an extended JSON API (options, explore, compare, FES table), typed from the OpenAPI schema and tested end to end; interconnector availability by price gap from hourly flows, tested out of sample (an option: it does not beat the flat share); data refreshed to October 2026; versioned docs and a Zenodo DOI v6.0 The daily gas price in the system model; a day-ahead forecast from NESO's demand and Elexon's wind forecasts, the gas price and auction prices (forecast: fundamentals); FES systems made secure to the reliability standard and a storage saturation study (openenergy system saturation); the battery optimiser in the browser (Battery Lab, Grid replay, 2035, Beat the battery); a Gymnasium environment; constraint evidence; an end-of-day energy target that is now exact (What's new) v6.1 The web app as a simulator: Britain's grid hour by hour with power flowing in by fuel and a battery trading on the in-browser optimiser, play controls, keys and a year strip; Play, 2035 and Research tabs; revenue after wear in the browser, so perfect foresight is a true ceiling; NESO's generation mix to October 2026 (What's new) v7.0 Real batteries: every GB grid battery's physical notifications, metered output and Balancing Mechanism volumes and cashflows from Elexon (2021 to October 2026), compared with the optimiser and by zone; Scotland and England & Wales demand, transfer and capacity by year; a Real batteries tab in the web app; the docs' headline numbers checked against their sources on every test run (What's new; current)

Planned

Release Scope v7.1 A two-zone dispatch model (Scotland and England & Wales) checked against the observed transfer, to value where a battery relieves constraints; the saturation study on every weather year from 2019, using capacity by year; the evening peak premium the cost-based model misses

Alongside releases: refresh and re-check the bundled data every release; keep CI and its actions current; revisit stochastic planning if an open, forecastable market price appears. Ideas are welcome in issues.

docs.title: availability_from_flows
docs.text:
availability_from_flows(system_dir, gb_prices, neighbours)

Per link, the share of a price taker's imports and exports that actually flowed.

A price taker on gb_prices (actual hourly GBP/MWh, the fitting years) imports at full capacity whenever GB is dearer than the neighbour and exports whenever it is cheaper, from the day the link entered service. Each share is the actual energy (Elexon) over that trade, at most 1. Modelled prices are never used. Links with no trade in the period get the mean of the others.

docs.title: availability_by_gap
docs.text:
availability_by_gap(system_dir, gb_prices, neighbours)

Per link and direction, the share of capacity used by size of the price gap.

Hours from the day each link entered service are binned by the gap between gb_prices (actual hourly GBP/MWh) and the neighbour's actual price, from the lower edges in GAP_EDGES: imports when GB is dearer, exports when cheaper. Each bin's share is the link's mean hourly flow that way (Elexon, hourly) over its capacity, made non-decreasing in the gap (weighted by hours) so that it can be offered as stepped capacity. Bins without hours take their neighbour's share. Modelled prices are never used. Columns: link, direction, gap_from, share, hours.

docs.title: openenergy.dispatch.arbitrage
docs.text: Single-battery energy arbitrage as a mixed-integer linear programme (HiGHS).

docs.title: DispatchConfig dataclass
docs.text:
Optimisation settings.

end_soc is a fraction of usable energy; None means return to the starting energy. max_cycles caps equivalent full cycles over the horizon (the backtest scales it by the days planned, so it stays a per-day cap). lookahead_days makes the backtest plan each day together with that many following days of forecasts, settling only the first; the end-energy target then applies at the end of the last day.

docs.title: DispatchPlan dataclass
docs.text:
Optimal schedule in MW per interval and stored energy at each boundary (T+1).

With frequency response, reserve_mw is MW held per block and service, and response_charge_mw/response_discharge_mw the expected average power it moves. expected_revenue covers energy; expected_response the availability payments.

docs.title: Reserve dataclass
docs.text:
Frequency-response options over a horizon.

block maps each interval to a row of price (-1 where nothing can be reserved). price (GBP/MW/h) and utilisation (MWh delivered per MW per hour) have one row per block and one column per service. fixed holds MW already committed (NaN where free). beyond_hours is how long each block runs past the horizon end; the plan keeps enough energy to stay idle through it. With energy_paid, delivered energy is bought or sold at the interval's price; otherwise it is free, as under NESO's ABSVD adjustment.

docs.title: Time and units
docs.text: Prices are a series on a regular UTC grid; each timestamp labels the start of its interval of length \(\Delta t\) hours. Power is in MW, energy in MWh and prices in currency per MWh. Days are UTC days.

docs.title: Battery physics
docs.text:
A battery has a power rating \(P\) (MW), a rated energy \(E_{rated}\) (MWh), charge and discharge efficiencies \(\eta_c, \eta_d\), and a state-of-charge window \([SOC_{min}, SOC_{max}]\) expressed as fractions of usable energy.

For charge \(c_t\) and discharge \(d_t\) (MW) in interval \(t\), stored energy evolves as

\[E_{t+1} = E_t + \eta_c\, c_t\, \Delta t - \frac{d_t\, \Delta t}{\eta_d}\]

Each interval adds its own throughput to the equivalent full cycle count:

\[N \mathrel{+}= \frac{(c_t + d_t)\,\Delta t}{2 E_{rated}}\]

State of health is computed from lifetime totals, so it never compounds:

\[SOH = 1 - k_{cycle}\, N - k_{calendar}\, \text{age in years}\]

Usable energy is \(E_{rated} \cdot SOH\). Ageing is applied at the end of every UTC day, including days that are not simulated.

docs.title: Dispatch
docs.text:
Each day is planned by maximising forecast revenue less an optional degradation cost \(\kappa\) per MWh of throughput:

\[\max \sum_t \hat p_t\, (d_t - c_t)\, \Delta t - \kappa \sum_t (c_t + d_t)\, \Delta t\]

With a carbon price \(\lambda\) (currency per tCO2), the planning price becomes \(\hat p_t + \lambda \hat e_t / 1000\) for planned carbon intensity \(\hat e_t\) in gCO2/kWh, so importing is dearer and exporting worth more when the grid is carbon-intensive. Reported revenue stays at market prices; see System analysis.

subject to the energy balance above for \(t = 0 \dots T-1\) with \(E_0\) fixed, and:

  • \(0 \le c_t \le P\, u_t\) and \(0 \le d_t \le P\,(1 - u_t)\) with \(u_t \in \{0, 1\}\), so the battery never charges and discharges at once (an LP would, to burn energy at negative prices);
  • \(SOC_{min}\, E_{usable} \le E_t \le SOC_{max}\, E_{usable}\);
  • \(E_T = E_{target}\), by default the energy the day started with;
  • optionally, \(\sum_t (c_t + d_t)\, \Delta t \le 2 N_{max}\, E_{usable}\).

The model is solved with HiGHS; a day takes a few milliseconds.

Try it: drag the prices and watch the plan change. Flatten them and the battery stops, because no gap covers its losses and wear; pull one evening hour up and it charges in the cheapest hours to sell into it. (The widget runs the same programme in your browser, from the web app; a 1 MW / 2 MWh battery, 95% each way, £5/MWh wear.)

If the widget does not load, open it at open-energy-eight.vercel.app/embed/arbitrage.

docs.title: Backtest timing
docs.text:
For each day \(D\):

  1. The forecaster receives the prices known at the decision time, lead_hours before the start of \(D\) (default 12, i.e. noon on \(D-1\)). With information: auction (the default since v6.0) that is every day whose day-ahead auction had cleared: GB's auction for a day runs in the late morning of the day before, so at noon on \(D-1\) all of \(D-1\)'s prices are known. information: decision keeps only prices for hours before the decision time, as before v6.0.
  2. The optimiser plans \(D\) on the forecast, together with the next lookahead_days days of forecasts if set (all made at the same decision time); the end-energy target then applies at the end of the last planned day.
  3. Only \(D\)'s part of the plan is applied through the battery physics and valued at actual prices.
  4. The battery state carries into \(D+1\), which is planned afresh.

Near the end of the data, or before a gap, the lookahead shortens to the days that can be forecast. With lookahead_days: 0 (the default) each day is planned alone and must end with the energy it started with.

Days with missing prices, or for which the forecaster has no usable history, are skipped and listed with the reason. Scenarios that are not perfect foresight also run a perfect-foresight benchmark on the same days.

docs.title: Forecasters
docs.text:
Method Description perfect_foresight The actual prices; the upper bound. naive_last_week The same interval seven days earlier, falling back to fourteen. noisy_foresight Actual prices plus seeded Gaussian error of a chosen spread. gradient_boosting Gradient-boosted trees on calendar features and 1/2/7/14-day lags (needs the forecast extra). fundamentals OpenEnergy's day-ahead forecast (v6.0): gradient-boosted trees retrained each month on what was known at the decision time (recent prices, NESO's day-ahead demand forecast, Elexon's day-ahead wind forecast, the daily gas price, the calendar), predicting each hour relative to the last day's mean price; each month's shape is stretched by the factor that earned a reference battery most over the previous 90 days. Needs the forecast extra, or path to the bundled precomputed forecast (data/forecasts/).

The gradient-boosting model masks any lag at or after the decision time in exactly the same way during training and forecasting, and is trained only on a window that ends before the backtest starts.

docs.title: Renewable plants
docs.text:
A plant has a technology, an installed capacity \(C\) and an annual degradation rate \(r\). Its available output follows the OPSD capacity factor \(cf_t\):

\[g_t = C \cdot cf_t \cdot (1 - r)^{\text{age}}\]

docs.title: Captured price
docs.text:
The captured price is what the market paid per MWh the plant actually produced; the capture rate compares it with the time-weighted (baseload) average:

\[\bar p_{cap} = \frac{\sum_t p_t\, g_t}{\sum_t g_t} \qquad \text{capture rate} = \frac{\bar p_{cap}}{\frac{1}{T}\sum_t p_t}\]

A capture rate below 100% means the technology tends to produce when prices are low; falling capture rates as a technology's share grows are known as cannibalisation. openenergy capture reports this per year, together with capacity factor and the share of output produced at negative prices.

docs.title: Co-located sites
docs.text:
A plant and a battery can share one grid connection with an export limit \(X\), an import limit \(I\) and an optional premium \(\pi\) per MWh of renewable output delivered (ROC- or CfD-like support).

flowchart LR
    G[Plant output] -->|y| Grid
    G -->|s| B[Battery]
    G -->|k| C[Curtailed]
    Grid -->|m| B
    B -->|d| Grid

Each interval, output \(G_t = y_t + s_t + k_t\) goes to the grid, to the battery, or is curtailed; the battery charges \(c_t = s_t + m_t\) from the plant and the grid (\(m_t \le I\)), and net export \(x_t = y_t + d_t - m_t \le X\). The daily plan maximises

\[\sum_t \left[\hat p_t\, x_t + \pi\,(y_t + s_t)\right]\Delta t - \kappa \sum_t (c_t + d_t)\,\Delta t\]

with the battery constraints above. Output is curtailed when the price falls below \(-\pi\) or the connection is full and the battery cannot absorb it.

Every site run is compared with the same plant and battery on separate connections: the plant exports up to its own capacity and the battery trades on its own. The difference is the co-location value; it is negative when a shared connection is too small, and should be weighed against the connection capacity saved.

Upper bound

Plans use the actual plant output (perfect generation foresight) and forecast prices. Co-location results are therefore an upper bound.

docs.title: Bundled extract
docs.text:
data/time_series/time_series_60min_singleindex_filtered.csv is an hourly extract of the Open Power System Data time-series package covering Great Britain from 31 December 2014 to 30 September 2020. It contains the GB day-ahead price (in GBP/MWh), load, and solar and wind generation and capacity. Timestamps are UTC (utc_timestamp). Version 2020-10-06 is still OPSD's latest time-series release (checked 13 October 2026), so later years come from the sources below.

Of 2,101 days, 2,085 have a complete set of prices. The gaps are two-hour holes on the spring clock change each year, two single missing hours, and four outages of about a day. With the default max_gap_hours: 2, the short gaps are interpolated and the outages are skipped.

Prices include genuine scarcity spikes, up to £999/MWh in September–November 2016; they are kept.

docs.title: GB prices after 2020
docs.text:
OPSD's GB prices stop in September 2020. data/prices/gb_day_ahead_ember.csv carries the GB hourly day-ahead price from 30 June 2016 to 28 October 2026 (90,553 hours, no gaps), from Ember's European wholesale price data (CC BY 4.0), stored in EUR/MWh as published. OpenEnergy converts each hour to GBP at the ECB reference rate for its day (data/prices/ecb_gbp_per_eur.csv; the latest earlier rate on weekends and holidays). Use it with data: {source: ember, path: ...}; openenergy data update downloads the latest months into a user cache.

Where both exist (July 2016 to September 2020, 37,239 hours) the converted Ember price matches OPSD with correlation 0.99996 and a mean absolute difference of £0.11/MWh, so the two can be joined. The system model's backcast does exactly that: OPSD where it has a price, Ember otherwise.

Year 2017 2018 2019 2020 2021 2022 2023 2024 2025 Mean £/MWh 45.3 57.4 42.9 35.3 117.8 204.8 94.1 72.5 80.7 Mean daily spread £/MWh 41.6 40.6 32.9 39.6 146.4 155.6 70.0 59.9 67.5

The series keeps 615 negative hours (down to −€60/MWh) and 38 hours at €1,000/MWh or more (up to €2,576/MWh in 2021–2022). From 2021 Ember takes the UK price from EMR Settlement, whose own reuse terms could not be read (the site blocks scripted access); OpenEnergy relies on Ember's CC BY 4.0 publication and cites both.

docs.title: Neighbouring markets
docs.text:
data/prices/europe_day_ahead_ember.csv holds the hourly day-ahead prices of the six markets GB's interconnectors reach (France, the Netherlands, Belgium, Norway, Denmark and Ireland), EUR/MWh as published by Ember, from 1 January 2015 (Ireland from 1 October 2018) to 30 October 2026. The system model's interconnector links trade at these prices, converted to GBP like the GB price.

Mean £/MWh (ECB rates) 2019 2020 2021 2022 2023 2024 2025 GB 42.9 35.3 117.8 204.8 94.1 72.5 80.7 France 34.6 28.7 93.4 235.1 84.4 48.9 52.2 Netherlands 36.1 28.7 88.1 206.2 83.5 65.3 74.3 Belgium 34.5 28.4 89.1 208.4 84.7 59.4 70.6 Norway 34.2 8.2 53.6 118.8 51.5 32.8 40.9 Denmark 34.2 23.5 75.4 184.0 73.7 59.8 69.9 Ireland 44.2 33.5 116.3 192.5 110.0 92.0 97.8

From 2023 to 2025 GB's mean price was above every neighbour's except Ireland's, which helps explain why price-taking links at full capacity import so much (each link's availability is therefore fitted from its flows; see below).

Known issues: Ember publishes one price for Norway and one for Denmark, without saying how the bidding zones are combined; GB's links land in southern Norway (NO2) and western Denmark (DK1). A few hours are blank on 31 July and 30 September 2026 (none before 2026).

docs.title: Renewable capacity factors
docs.text:
The extract also has hourly capacity-factor profiles (generation divided by installed capacity) for solar, wind, wind_onshore and wind_offshore, from 2015 to 29 December 2019; OPSD stops publishing capacity after that.

In 233 hours the solar profile exceeds 1.0 (up to 1.367): reported capacity lags new build, so generation divided by capacity overshoots. OpenEnergy clips profiles to [0, 1] and reports how many values were clipped. The same lag pushes GB solar capacity factors to 15–18%, above the roughly 11% usually quoted; this changes absolute output but not capture rates, which depend on the shape of the profile.

Other OPSD zones can be used by pointing data.path at a larger OPSD time_series_*_singleindex.csv. OPSD publishes GB prices in GBP and all other zones in EUR; OpenEnergy labels the currency accordingly.

docs.title: Carbon intensity
docs.text:
data/carbon_intensity/gb_national.csv holds GB national carbon intensity for every half-hour from 1 January 2018 to 29 October 2026: NESO's forecast and its estimated actual, in gCO2/kWh. It was downloaded with scripts/fetch_carbon_intensity.py and is stored exactly as published; 179 half-hours the API did not return are left blank.

The archive has 804 half-hours without an actual value (18 runs, the longest about three days) and 16 implausible forecasts (up to 13,579 gCO2/kWh). OpenEnergy treats any value outside 0–1000 gCO2/kWh as missing and reports how many it rejected. Annual mean actual intensity falls from 248 (2018) to 214 (2019), 180 (2020), 188 (2021), 183 (2022), 152 (2023), 125 (2024), 129 (2025) and 122 gCO2/kWh (2026 to 12 October).

These are average intensities of the whole system. Storage and renewables change the marginal plant, whose emissions can differ; emissions results in OpenEnergy show direction and rough scale, not causal impact.

docs.title: GB system data
docs.text:
data/system/, written by scripts/fetch_system_data.py, feeds the system model:

File Contents Source generation_mix.csv Half-hourly GB generation by fuel, MW, 2015-01-01 to 2026-10-29 (207,360 rows, no gaps) NESO historic generation mix fleet.csv GB capacity at each year end 2014–2025 (CCGT, coal, gas turbines, oil engines, nuclear, pumped storage) and CCGT and coal efficiency DUKES 5.8 and 5.10 fuel_prices.csv Quarterly coal, oil and gas prices paid by major power producers, 2014–2025; the model's gas price before 2018 and with gas_price: quarterly DESNZ QEP 3.2.1 carbon_prices.csv EU ETS (2015–2020) and UK ETS (2021–2025) price on 1 April with ECB exchange rates, and carbon price support rates World Bank, DESNZ (2021), ECB, HMRC unit_parameters.csv Unit size, minimum stable output and start-up cost for CCGT, coal and peaking plant (unit commitment) Danish Energy Agency, NREL, ECB interconnectors.csv GB's ten built interconnectors: neighbour, import and export capacity (MW) NESO Interconnector Register, 12 October 2026 interconnector_flows.csv Daily imports and exports per link, MWh, 2016-01-01 to 2026-10-29 Elexon BMRS FUELHH interconnector_flows_hourly.csv Hourly net flow per link, MW, 2019-01-01 to 2026-10-29 Elexon BMRS FUELHH interconnector_availability.csv Each link's import and export availability: actual flow over a price taker's trade on actual prices, 2019–2025 Elexon BMRS FUELHH, Ember, OPSD, ECB interconnector_gap_availability.csv Each link's share of capacity used by size of the price gap (option availability: gap), 2019–2025 Elexon BMRS FUELHH, Ember, OPSD, ECB

The model's inputs stop at the latest complete calendar year, 2025 (checked 13 October 2026): DUKES publishes a year's fleet the following July, so 2026 has none yet, and the 2026 fuel and carbon prices that exist are not added until the year is complete, so every model year has the same kind of inputs.

Known issues: NESO fills gaps by seasonal decomposition and sets net-negative values to zero, so pumping demand and net exports are absent; transmission solar and batteries are in "other". DUKES efficiencies are UK-wide averages. One ETS price per year misses moves within the year (EU ETS 2018 rose from about €10 to €25; UK ETS 2021–2023 swung more). The World Bank dashboard has no UK ETS price on 1 April 2021, before the first auction, so 2021 uses DESNZ's 2021 carbon price (mean auction price, £47.96/t). DESNZ suppresses some coal prices from 2023 (carried forward) and gives no coal efficiency for 2025 (latest earlier value used). Quarterly fuel prices are what power producers paid, including contracts agreed earlier, so they lag market gas prices; since v6.0 the model uses the daily wholesale gas price from 2018 instead (below, and the system model). Emission factors (gas 0.1839, coal 0.3096 tCO2 per MWh of fuel) follow from the carbon price support rates, which are set at £18/tCO2.

The interconnector register holds today's capacities only. Each link's first day in service comes from its flows (the first flow in the first 14 days carrying at least a fifth of its capacity, which skips commissioning tests): Nemo Link 2019-01-30, IFA2 2021-01-22, NS Link 2021-09-23, ElecLink 2022-05-23, Viking Link 2023-12-29 and Greenlink 2025-01-19. The flows also show limits the register does not (Moyle about 300 MW in 2016–2017, IFA about half its capacity in 2022, BritNed never above about 1,050 of 1,200 MW), so modelled link capacity is overstated in those periods.

Each link's availability (scripts/fit_interconnector_availability.py) is the energy it actually moved (Elexon) over what a price taker would have moved at full capacity on actual GB and neighbour day-ahead prices, per direction, capped at 1. It uses actual prices and flows only. Fitted on 2019–2022 it gives 36.9 TWh of imports in 2024 (actual 43.9, full capacity 66.0) and 11.8 TWh of exports (actual 10.6); the published file is fitted on 2019–2025.

docs.title: What is known the day before
docs.text:
data/fundamentals/, written by scripts/fetch_fundamentals.py (or openenergy data update --fundamentals), holds what is published before the day-ahead auction, each with the time it was issued so a backtest uses only what existed at its decision time:

File Contents Source gas_sap_daily.csv Daily System Average Price of gas, p/kWh, 2018-01-01 to 2026-10-25 (3,220 days, no gaps) ONS, from National Gas Transmission neso_demand_day_ahead.csv NESO's day-ahead national demand forecast at its cardinal points, with issue times, 2018-01-02 to 2026-11-01 (58,792 points) NESO Day Ahead Demand Forecast elexon_wind_day_ahead.csv Elexon's hourly wind forecast, the latest issued by noon UTC the day before, 2018-01-02 to 2026-11-01 (76,970 hours) Elexon BMRS WINDFOR

The system model uses the daily gas price from its first day (quarterly DESNZ prices before); the fundamentals forecast uses all three. Known issues: SAP is a wholesale price without the network charges power stations pay; NESO's demand forecast covers transmission demand and its published times fit best an hour earlier (used as published); NESO's own wind forecast archive keeps only the latest issue for each half-hour, often made on the day, so Elexon's is used. Details in data/fundamentals/README.md.

data/forecasts/gb_fundamentals_day_ahead.csv is model output, not source data: the fundamentals forecast for every hour from 2019 to 28 October 2026, exactly as a backtest would make it, so scenarios and the web app can use it without training (data/forecasts/README.md; built by scripts/build_fundamentals_forecast.py).

docs.title: Future Energy Scenarios
docs.text:
data/fes/ holds NESO's Future Energy Scenarios tables unchanged, written by scripts/fetch_fes.py: the electricity supply (ES1) and demand summary (ED1) tables of FES: Pathways to Net Zero 2025 (pathways Holistic Transition, Electric Engagement, Hydrogen Evolution and Falling Behind, plus the Ten Year Forecast; 2024–2050) and of the 2026 Ten Year Outlook (2025–2036). system.fes uses their capacities (MW), storage (GWh) and annual system demand; see forward scenarios. FES 2025's 2025 column is already a projection and differs by pathway; FES publishes no fuel or carbon prices and no storage efficiencies.

data/scenarios/ is model output, not source data: hourly modelled prices for each pathway in 2030 and 2035 on 2025's weather (fes_prices.csv) and a summary next to FES's own figures (fes_summary.csv), written by scripts/build_scenario_prices.py for the web app, and the storage saturation study (saturation.csv, saturation_years.csv, from openenergy system saturation; see forward scenarios). data/app/ is model output too: per-MW battery results for common requests (1, 2 and 4 hours, every year, forecast, response option and pathway), written by scripts/build_app_results.py so the app answers at once. web/public/data/ reshapes bundled data and these results into the static files the app's in-browser pages read (scripts/build_app_data.py), each carrying its attribution.

docs.title: Frequency response
docs.text:
data/response/, written by scripts/fetch_response_data.py, feeds revenue stacking:

  • gb_dynamic_response.csv: the clearing price (GBP/MW/h) and cleared volume (MW) of each dynamic response service (DC, DM, DR; low and high) for every four-hour EFA block from 15 September 2021 22:00 to 30 October 2026 19:00 UTC (11,226 blocks, no gaps). DM and DR start on 26 March 2022.
  • gb_response_utilisation.csv: for each month from September 2021 to September 2026, the average share of contracted MW each service delivers (MWh per MW per hour), from NESO's one-second GB frequency and the delivery envelopes in NESO's Response Services Service Terms (version 6). The raw frequency files (about 75 MB a month) are not bundled.

Known issues: Dynamic Containment before 16 September 2021 was bought pay-as-bid and is not included; some prices are negative (mostly DM and DR high); utilisation is the delivery of a unit following the envelope exactly. See data/response/README.md.

docs.title: Imbalance prices
docs.text: data/balancing/gb_system_prices.csv, written by scripts/fetch_system_prices.py, holds the GB system (imbalance) price for every half-hour from 2016 to 29 October 2026 (189,840 periods, 20 blank where Elexon's API returned nothing). GB has a single imbalance price, so the sell and buy prices are equal; it is used by examples/imbalance_value.py.

docs.title: Transmission constraints
docs.text: data/constraints/, written by scripts/fetch_constraints.py, holds the evidence on the constraints page; no model uses it yet: constraint_breakdown_daily.csv, NESO's daily constraint costs and volumes from April 2021 (values unchanged), and day_ahead_boundaries_monthly.csv, a monthly summary of NESO's half-hourly day-ahead limits and flows by boundary group from January 2023. Known issues are in data/constraints/README.md.

docs.title: Real batteries
docs.text: data/fleet/, written by scripts/fetch_fleet.py from Elexon's BMRS, holds what GB's grid batteries did (Real batteries): battery_units.csv, the 83 BM units named as batteries with capacity, region and zone; battery_daily.csv, each unit's physical notifications, metered output (B1610), Balancing Mechanism volumes and cashflows and imbalance, by UTC day, January 2021 to 29 October 2026 (64,203 unit-days); and fleet_hourly.csv, the fleet each hour. scripts/real_batteries.py adds the yearly comparison with the optimiser. Read them with openenergy.data.batteries.RealBatteries. Known issues are in data/fleet/README.md.

docs.title: Zones
docs.text: data/zones/, written by scripts/fetch_zones.py: demand_by_zone.csv, GB, England and Wales and Scottish demand, the transfer from Scotland (from 2023) and embedded wind and solar each half-hour from 2019 (NESO historic demand data), and capacity_by_year.csv, grid-scale battery, solar and wind capacity by zone and year (DESNZ REPD). Used on the constraints page; no model uses them yet.

docs.title: Software
docs.text:
The system model's storage dispatch uses PyPSA:

T. Brown, J. Hörsch, D. Schlachtberger. PyPSA: Python for Power System Analysis. Journal of Open Research Software 6(1), 2018. https://doi.org/10.5334/jors.188.

Optimisation problems are solved with HiGHS (MIT licence); the web app's in-browser optimiser uses highs-js, HiGHS compiled to WebAssembly (MIT licence).

Each data folder has a README.md with the full source, licence and known issues, and every summary.json repeats the attribution for the data a run used.

docs.title: Findings
docs.text: What OpenEnergy's runs show so far, each with the page that has the method, the numbers and the limits. Every number here comes from a command or script in the repository and was re-run for v6.0 (v6.1 changed only the web app; v7.0 added real batteries and zones). The headline tables are checked against their source files on every test run (tests/test_docs_numbers.py).

docs.title: A battery on GB day-ahead prices
docs.text: A 1 MW / 2 MWh battery planning on last week's prices earned £13,943 per MW-year in 2019, £76,948 in the 2022 gas crisis and £35,861 in 2025, keeping 71–83% of what perfect foresight allows every year from 2017 (Home). Try any day:

docs.title: Real batteries trade the same shape, far less of it
docs.text: GB's real grid batteries, from Elexon's metered data, discharged about 400 full-power hours a year in 2024 and 2025, at the same hours a day-ahead optimiser uses, but the energy they moved was worth only 17–23% of what a 1-hour optimiser on OpenEnergy's forecast earns at the day-ahead price. With their contracts priced at the day-ahead price, the Balancing Mechanism and imbalance, they made an estimated £16,200–16,700 per MW-year, before frequency response. Scottish batteries end up with about the same total as English and Welsh ones, paid more for selling ahead and less in the BM (Real batteries).

docs.title: A better forecast pays, less than its error suggests
docs.text: OpenEnergy's day-ahead forecast (demand and wind forecasts, the daily gas price and recent prices, as known the day before) halves the error of last week's prices from 2023 and keeps 86–89% of perfect-foresight revenue instead of 74–81%. In 2021, when gas prices rose faster than any model trained on earlier years could follow, last week's prices did better (Research). A reinforcement-learning agent given the same information kept 27–38% (Research).

docs.title: Storage saturates, and does little for a cold, still week
docs.text: On FES 2035 systems made secure to the 3-hour reliability standard, a battery joining NESO's own fleet earns about a third of what the first battery would (Falling Behind: £15,551 against £43,609 per MW-year), and each MW of that fleet replaces 0.09–0.16 MW of firm capacity in the pathways that need it (Forward scenarios):

docs.title: The model follows the gas crisis, not its evening peaks
docs.text: With the daily gas price, the cost-based model of GB's plants follows the 2022 gas crisis with a correlation of 0.81 against actual prices (0.40 with quarterly prices), but its daily spread stays a fraction of the market's in 2021–2022 (System model). Fuel prices do not explain the gap; scarcity pricing and bidding above cost, which open data does not describe, are left out rather than fitted.

docs.title: Frequency response, then arbitrage
docs.text: Selling Dynamic Containment alongside day-ahead trading raised a 2-hour battery's revenue by 58–156% a year in 2022–2025, with fewer cycles. Re-planning against imbalance prices without a forecast of them gained in some years and lost in others (Revenue stacking).

docs.title: Constraints are growing, outside the day-ahead price
docs.text:
NESO's thermal constraint costs rose from £1.1 billion in 2021/22 to £2.0 billion in 2025/26, and six boundary groups were at their day-ahead limit a third to a half of the time from 2024 (Constraints). GB's price is national, so this changes balancing costs, not the day-ahead values above.

If an embedded page does not load, open the web app.

docs.title: 7.0: from the model to the real grid
docs.text:
OpenEnergy 7.0 checks its optimiser against what GB's real batteries did and adds the data for Scotland and England & Wales. No model default changes; every 6.x result stands.

  • Real batteries (guide, web app): every GB grid battery's physical notifications, metered output and Balancing Mechanism volumes and cashflows from Elexon, January 2021 to October 2026 (data/fleet/, scripts/fetch_fleet.py, openenergy.data.batteries). In 2024 and 2025 the real fleet discharged about 400 full-power hours a year at the hours the optimiser uses, but its metered energy was worth 17–23% of a 1-hour optimiser's day-ahead revenue on OpenEnergy's forecast; with contracts priced at the day-ahead price, the BM and imbalance it made an estimated £16,200–16,700 per MW-year, before frequency response. A physical notification turned out not to be what a battery did (one unit notified 1,262 MWh out and metered 615 in a week), so physical operation comes from the meter.
  • Scotland and England & Wales (constraints): zonal demand and the transfer across the B6 boundary from NESO, and grid-scale capacity by zone and year from DESNZ's project register (data/zones/, scripts/fetch_zones.py). Scotland sent power south in 86% of half-hours in 2025 (19.3 TWh), up from 71% in 2023. Scottish batteries make about the same per MW as English and Welsh ones, by selling ahead and being paid less in the BM.
  • The web app gains a Real batteries tab (each year's fleet against the optimiser, its average day, every unit by zone) and shows the real fleet's output each hour in the simulator.
  • Numbers checked on every test run: tests/test_docs_numbers.py recomputes the headline tables (saturation, the Scottish transfer, real batteries) from their source files. Its first run found two errors in the docs, both fixed: Ten Year Forecast was called a pathway with no shortfall (it needs 0.75 GW of firm capacity without batteries), and a transfer maximum was mis-rounded.

Planned for 7.1: a two-zone dispatch model checked against the observed transfer, and the saturation study on 2019–2023 weather using the capacity by year.

docs.title: 6.1: the web app becomes a simulator
docs.text:
OpenEnergy 6.1 changes only the web app and its data; the library, the API and every model result are as in 6.0.

  • One simulator instead of pages. open-energy-eight.vercel.app opens on Britain's grid hour by hour: each fuel flows into the GB node with a band as wide as its output, the node shows the day-ahead price, and your battery charges and discharges on a plan the optimiser makes in the browser. Play at 1, 4 or 24 hours a second, step with the arrow keys, or click a day on the year strip (each day coloured by its price spread). A side panel sets the battery, the forecast it plans with and the day, and shows the day and the whole year for all three forecasts.
  • Four tabs: Simulator, Play, 2035 and Research. Play lets you paint a day's plan, then run the day and watch actual prices and the scores come in; it keeps the engine's rule that the battery starts and ends the day half full. 2035 counts the saturation study's value up and down as you add batteries. Research holds the analyst pages (/run, /result, /explore, /compare, /scenarios), unchanged.
  • Revenue after wear in the browser. The 6.0 Battery Lab compared revenue before wear, so on days when a forecast's plan traded more it could show more than perfect foresight (on 20 October 2026 a 1 MW / 2 MWh battery on OpenEnergy's forecast showed 113%). The simulator now compares revenue less wear, the quantity the optimiser maximises, so perfect foresight is the most any plan earns (90% that day). The Python backtest and the API's year results are unchanged.
  • 2026 on the grid. NESO's generation mix now runs to 29 October 2026; the rows to 2025 are unchanged, and the system model still uses 2015–2025.
  • Addresses. /lab and /replay open the simulator with their day and battery, so 6.0 links keep working; sources are one click away under each view. The app and the docs use the README's logo.

OpenEnergy 6.0 makes the model more accurate, answers a research question, and puts the battery optimiser in the browser. Three defaults changed, and one bug was fixed that moves results; this section lists each with what it does to the numbers, measured by re-running every result in these docs.

docs.title: New
docs.text:
• A day-ahead forecast built on fundamentals (forecast: fundamentals): NESO's day-ahead demand forecast, Elexon's day-ahead wind forecast, the daily gas price and recent prices, each only as published by the decision time, in a model retrained every month. From 2023 it halves the error of last week's prices, and a 1 MW / 2 MWh battery planning on it keeps 86–89% of the perfect-foresight revenue instead of 74–81% (Research). The forecast for every hour since 2019 is bundled (data/forecasts/).
  • How much storage can GB use? openenergy system saturation scales each FES 2035 battery fleet from none to three times FES's figure on a secure system: the first half of the fleet takes half or more of a battery's value away, and each MW of FES batteries replaces only 0.09–0.16 MW of firm capacity in a cold, still spell (Forward scenarios).
  • The optimiser in your browser: the web app gains a live home page, the Battery Lab (any day, battery and forecast, with the whole year solved in the background), Grid replay, the 2035 study and Beat the battery. They run the same daily programme in TypeScript on HiGHS compiled to WebAssembly, tested against the Python backtest. Concepts has a widget to drag prices and watch the plan.
  • A reinforcement-learning environment (openenergy.rl, pip install 'openenergy[rl]'): a Gymnasium environment with the optimiser as the baseline. An agent trained in the design work kept 27–38% of perfect-foresight revenue where the optimiser kept 78–83%, so "forecast, then optimise" stays (Research).
  • Data: the daily System Average Price of gas (ONS), NESO's day-ahead demand forecast and Elexon's day-ahead wind forecast, each with issue times (data/fundamentals/, openenergy data update --fundamentals; Data).

docs.title: Changed defaults
docs.text:
Setting Before 6.0 To keep the old behaviour Gas price in the system model DESNZ quarterly price paid Daily System Average Price from 2018 system.gas_price: quarterly What a forecaster knows at the decision time Prices for hours before it Every day whose auction had cleared (at noon on D−1, all of D−1) information: decision FES systems As FES gives them Least firm capacity added to meet 3 hours' loss of load fes.adequacy: as_modelled

Daily gas. The backcast follows the gas crisis much better: the merit order's error falls by 31–42% in 2021–2024 and its correlation with actual prices rises from 0.40 to 0.81 in 2022 and from 0.10 to 0.53 in 2024. Before the crisis the change is mixed (the 2019 mean is £4.2 lower, now £4.8 below actual), and the missing daily spread is unchanged (System model). FES results and every system scenario from 2018 change with it.

Auction information. Last week's prices, perfect foresight and the gradient-boosting forecaster never used the previous afternoon's prices, so their results do not change. The fundamentals forecaster uses them.

Secure FES systems. Holistic Transition, Electric Engagement and Hydrogen Evolution 2035 get 6.25–9.25 GW of firm capacity, and their unserved energy falls from 215–715 GWh to 7–13 GWh. Their mean prices fall from £120–211/MWh to £73–76/MWh, and a battery's perfect-foresight value on them from 1.8–2.7 times the model's own 2025 to about it or below (Forward scenarios).

docs.title: Fixed: the end-of-day energy target
docs.text:
The daily plan required the battery to end each day with at least the energy it began with. When the last hour was cheap, a plan could end fuller, and the next day's target was then that fuller level, so the battery kept ratcheting up and holding energy it could have sold. The plan now ends exactly at the target (\(E_T = E_{target}\), Concepts).

The effect depends on how often the last hour is cheap on the forecast:

  • Last week's prices: under 0.3% a year (2017: £20,682 to £20,633 per MW-year; 2019: £13,936 to £13,943).
  • Revenue stacking: up to 2% (2025 with DC, DM and DR, energy unpaid: £89,807 to £90,766; with energy at day-ahead prices, £127,976 to £125,634).
  • Re-planning every half-hour on imbalance prices, where each re-plan set a new target: the result changed sign in three of four years, from losing 6–39% against day-ahead to +18%, +17%, +1% and −12% (Revenue stacking).
  • The fundamentals forecast in its design stage: a 2024 capture ratio of 73.7% became 85.3%.

docs.title: The web app
docs.text: The year form moved from / to /run; /result, /explore, /compare and /scenarios keep their addresses, so shared links still work. The app offers the fundamentals forecast for historic years from 2019, and the FES table shows the firm capacity each pathway needed.

docs.title: Numbers re-run
docs.text: Every table and number in these docs was re-run for 6.0 with the commands and scripts named next to it. The ones that moved by more than rounding are on the pages linked above; the Research and Revenue stacking tables move by under 2% except where noted.

docs.title: openenergy sweep
docs.text:
uv run openenergy sweep examples/gb-2019-naive.yaml \
  --set battery.energy_mwh=1,2,4 --set dispatch.degradation_cost=0,5 [--out sweep.csv]

Runs a scenario for every combination of --set dotted.key=v1,v2 values (up to 100) and ranks them by total revenue. For a system scenario it keeps the order given and reports price, emissions, curtailment, cost and any battery's revenue.

docs.title: openenergy system validate
docs.text:
uv run openenergy system validate [--start 2015-04-01] [--end 2020-09-30] [--out backcast/]
uv run openenergy system validate --start 2021-01-01 --end 2025-12-31
uv run openenergy system validate --commitment --price start

Rebuilds GB prices and gas and coal output from fuel, carbon and fleet data, and compares each year with what happened: mean, MAE, correlation, 95th percentile and average daily spread of price, gas and coal output, and CO2. The system data runs to the end of 2025. Actual prices come from the bundled OPSD file and, after it ends in September 2020, the Ember file; --prices (repeatable, earlier files first) points at other copies. --commitment adds start-up costs and minimum stable output (unit commitment; about a minute per year). --price start compares the start price instead of the marginal price and needs --commitment. --data points at another copy of data/system. --out writes backcast.csv, hourly.csv and summary.json.

docs.title: openenergy system run
docs.text:
uv run openenergy system run examples/gb-2019-system.yaml [--out outputs/gb-2019-system]

Dispatches one GB year with a scenario's changes and prints price, generation by technology, curtailment, emissions, system cost and, if the scenario has a battery, its revenue on the modelled prices. Writes dispatch.csv and summary.json. Scenarios with storage need the system extra (uv sync --extra system).

docs.title: openenergy data info
docs.text:
uv run openenergy data info data/time_series/time_series_60min_singleindex_filtered.csv

Lists each price zone with its currency, date range and number of complete days.

docs.title: openenergy data update
docs.text:
uv run openenergy data update [--dir DIR]

Downloads the latest GB hourly day-ahead prices from Ember (CC BY 4.0, in EUR as published) and the ECB's daily GBP rates into DIR (default ~/.cache/openenergy/prices, or $XDG_CACHE_HOME/openenergy/prices). Point a scenario at the result with data: {source: ember, path: DIR/gb_day_ahead_ember.csv}. The bundled copy in data/prices/ is refreshed by scripts/fetch_prices.py.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: Invalid scenarios, missing files and infeasible plans print a single error: line and exit with status 1.

docs.title: Transmission constraints
docs.text: GB has one national wholesale price (DESNZ, REMA summer update, July 2025), and OpenEnergy models GB as one bus. The transmission network does not behave like one: when wind in the north exceeds what the lines south can carry, NESO pays generators on one side of the boundary to turn down and others to turn up. That changes balancing costs and where a battery helps, not the day-ahead price. This page collects what open data says about it, before any model of it (data/constraints/, written by scripts/fetch_constraints.py).

docs.title: What constraints cost
docs.text:
NESO's daily constraint costs, by financial year (April to March), GBP million:

Year Thermal Voltage System inertia Largest loss Total Thermal volume (TWh, net) 2021/22 1,134 111 60 115 1,420 −3.9 2022/23 1,504 141 104 6 1,754 −4.1 2023/24 1,040 268 83 0 1,390 −6.3 2024/25 1,710 154 41 0 1,905 −12.1 2025/26 1,956 212 41 0 2,210 −14.0 2026/27 (to 21 October) 1,607 171 31 0 1,808 −7.7

Thermal constraints (lines at their limit) are 75–90% of the cost. The net energy turned down for them more than tripled from 2022/23 to 2025/26, from 4.1 to 14.0 TWh, while their cost rose by 30%, so the cost per MWh of net volume fell from about £370 to £140.

docs.title: How often the boundaries are full
docs.text:
NESO publishes, a day ahead, each boundary group's limit and flow for every half-hour (from 2023). Share of half-hours with the flow at or above 95% of the limit, for the groups published in most half-hours:

Boundary group 2023 2024 2025 2026 (to October) SCOTEX 0.4% 25.4% 34.0% 41.9% SSHARN (2023), SSHARN3 22.1% 40.8% 32.5% 48.9% SSE_SP (2023), SSE_SP2 8.2% 49.3% 42.4% 53.7% SSEN_S 6.3% 34.0% 44.8% 51.8% HARSPNBLY 9.1% 35.2% 38.4% 42.2% NKILGRMO 15.0% 30.9% 40.4% 30.4% FLOWSTH 0.6% 4.7% 5.6% 7.4% GM_SNOW5A 2.2% 6.1% 4.7% 5.0% SEIMP (2023), SEIMPPR23 0.0% 2.4% 3.9% 3.9%

Six groups are at their limit a third to a half of the time from 2024; three seldom are. NESO's network diagrams, published with the data, show where each boundary runs. One caution: in 2023 almost no flow is above its limit, and from 2024 a fifth to a half are in the first six groups. NESO's description does not say whether the published flow is before or after its actions, so part of the jump may be in what is published. Group names also change (SSHARN became SSHARN3).

docs.title: Scotland and England & Wales
docs.text:
Most of GB's wind is in Scotland and most of its demand is not. NESO's historic demand data split national demand into England and Wales and the rest, and from 2023 publish the flow from Scotland to England and Wales (the transfer across the B6 boundary); DESNZ's Renewable Energy Planning Database gives where the grid-scale capacity is (data/zones/, scripts/fetch_zones.py):

Year Scotland's demand (mean GW) Transfer south (mean GW) Transfer, 95th percentile / highest (GW) Half-hours exporting south Energy sent south (TWh) 2023 2.19 1.36 4.53 / 6.24 71% 13.3 2024 2.13 1.96 5.26 / 6.70 83% 18.2 2025 2.16 2.11 4.96 / 6.59 86% 19.3 2026 (to 10 Oct) 2.05 2.34 5.06 / 6.71 91% 16.2 Grid-scale capacity at the end of 2025 (GW) Scotland England and Wales Onshore wind 10.1 4.1 Offshore wind 4.3 11.7 Batteries 0.6 3.6 Solar (over 150 kW) 0.1 10.4

Scotland uses about 2.2 GW on average and has over 14 GW of wind, so it sends power south most of the time, more each year, and the transfer tops out near 6.7 GW. What a battery north or south of the boundary actually earns is on Real batteries.

docs.title: What this means for OpenEnergy
docs.text:
• Day-ahead prices are national, so constraints do not change the backcasts or the battery values on day-ahead prices.
  • They do change where storage is worth most to the system: a battery on the exporting side of a full boundary can absorb wind that would otherwise be paid to turn down. v7.0 measures this from what real batteries in each zone earned; a two-zone dispatch model, checked against the transfer above, is planned for v7.1.
  • FES curtailment in the forward scenarios is curtailment on one bus; a real network would curtail more.

docs.title: Forward scenarios
docs.text:
The system model rebuilds GB prices from the plants behind them. v4.0 adds two things that let it look forward, and v4.2 makes the links behave as they have and adds unit commitment to them:

  • Interconnector links (system.interconnectors: links): GB's ten interconnectors trade with France, the Netherlands, Belgium, Norway, Denmark and Ireland at those markets' actual day-ahead prices, instead of holding imports at their historic output.
  • NESO Future Energy Scenarios (system.fes): a FES pathway's capacities and demand for a year from 2025 to 2035, applied to a historic weather year.

v6.0 makes each FES system secure to GB's reliability standard before valuing anything on it, and asks how much storage GB can use (below).

uv sync --extra system
uv run openenergy system run examples/gb-2035-holistic.yaml

name: gb-2035-holistic
system:
  data: ../data/system
  year: 2025                     # the weather year: weather, demand shape, fuel and carbon prices
  interconnectors: links         # or {mode: links, hurdle_gbp_per_mwh: 5, availability: 1.0}
  commitment: true               # start-up costs and minimum stable output (marginal price)
  fes:
    pathway: Holistic Transition # also Electric Engagement, Hydrogen Evolution, Falling Behind,
                                 # Ten Year Forecast (FES 2025) and Ten Year Outlook (2026)
    year: 2035                   # 2025 to 2035, not before the weather year
    battery_efficiency: 0.85     # round trip; FES publishes none (stated assumption)
    ldes_efficiency: 0.75        # round trip for new long-duration storage (stated assumption)
    adequacy: secure             # add the least firm capacity meeting lole_hours (v6.0); or as_modelled
    lole_hours: 3                # GB's reliability standard: hours a year with unserved energy
    # firm_mw: 8000              # or add exactly this much firm capacity, no search
    battery_scale: 1.0           # multiply the FES battery fleet's power
battery: {power_mw: 1, energy_mwh: 2}

Results are "this fleet and demand in 2025's weather and markets", not price forecasts: FES publishes no fuel or carbon price paths, so the weather year keeps its own.

docs.title: Interconnector links
docs.text:
Each built link in NESO's Interconnector Register is a price taker on GB's single bus: it imports up to its import capacity whenever GB's price is above the neighbour's actual day-ahead price (Ember, converted at ECB rates) plus a hurdle, and exports when GB's price is below the neighbour's minus the hurdle. A link joins the system on the day it entered service, read from Elexon's flows (Nemo Link 2019, IFA2 and NS Link 2021, ElecLink 2022, Viking Link at the end of 2023, Greenlink 2025). Historic imports are dropped. Irish prices start in October 2018, so links need a year from 2019. Links work with the merit order, PyPSA (when storage is added) and unit commitment.

At full capacity links trade far more than happened: imports up to 64% too high (2023) and exports up to 4.5 times too high (2021). A price taker sees every hour's price gap as profit; real flows are limited by outages, losses, ramping, capacity sold ahead, trading on later markets and the neighbours' own supply. Each link's availability (below) brings imports to within 5% of actual in 2022, 2024 and 2025; they are 10% high in 2023 and 17–29% low in 2019–2021. Exports are within 2% in 2022 and 10–22% low in 2023–2025, but about twice actual in 2019–2021: with the daily gas price the modelled GB price in those years is lower than actual, so the links export more and import less than they did.

Matching flows takes spread away: links at full capacity were importing the neighbours' daily shape, which partly hid the model's own flat price (2025: 39.1 at full capacity, 23.8 at fitted availability). Unit commitment restores the shape on GB's own plant: the spread is 63% to 88% of actual in 2019–2020 and 2023–2025 (30% and 38% in the 2021–2022 gas crisis, even with the daily gas price). The mean is £4.5–4.9 below actual in 2019–2020, £2–6 above it in 2023–2025 and £19–29 below it in 2021–2022 (see the system model).

docs.title: Link availability
docs.text: scripts/fit_interconnector_availability.py sets each link's import and export availability to the energy it actually moved over what a price taker at full capacity would have moved on actual GB and neighbour prices, 2019–2025, capped at 1 (see Data). Fitted only on flows, never on prices. Fitted on 2019–2022 instead, it gives 36.9 TWh of imports in 2024 against 43.9 actual (66.0 at full capacity), and 11.8 TWh of exports against 10.6. It is one number per link and direction, so it does not respond to the size of the price gap.

docs.title: Availability by price gap (v5.0)
docs.text:
Real links trade more of a bigger gap. From hourly flows (Elexon, 2019–2025) and actual prices, availability: gap takes each link's share of capacity in hours whose gap was £0–5, £5–10, £10–20, £20–40, £40–80 and over £80/MWh, made non-decreasing so each link can be offered as six steps, the k-th at the neighbour's price plus the bin's lower edge. Nemo Link, for example, imports 49% of its capacity at gaps under £5 and 90% above £80; IFA2 exports 12% and 78%. The Irish links barely respond. The shares are in data/system/interconnector_gap_availability.csv.

Tested the same way as the flat share (both fitted on 2019–2022 flows and actual prices, links in service before 2023), it follows the hour-to-hour flows a little better and the yearly energy a little worse:

Year Imports: actual / gap / flat Exports: actual / gap / flat Hourly correlation with actual flow: gap / flat 2023 33.5 / 24.4 / 26.7 10.1 / 8.0 / 10.0 0.47 / 0.43 2024 38.9 / 29.1 / 30.2 9.2 / 6.0 / 7.1 0.41 / 0.37 2025 38.9 / 28.6 / 29.3 9.5 / 6.2 / 7.4 0.46 / 0.43

In the model (links and unit commitment, 2023–2025) it moves the mean by under £1/MWh, lowers the daily spread by 2.1 to 3.4 (2025: 47.9 against 51.0), cuts exports by about a quarter, and changes the battery's perfect-foresight value by −10% to −7% (planning on last week's prices it earns 6% to 23% more). Because it does not beat the flat share out of sample, flows stays the default and gap is an option. It matters most for the FES pathways below, where links are short at scarcity.

docs.title: Marginal or start price
docs.text:
With links and commitment, the marginal price is closer to history than the start price in 2023, 2024 and 2025 on the mean, the daily spread and battery value; the start price holds the night up at a running unit's cost plus its start cost. The scenarios below use the marginal price. This is a choice between two un-fitted definitions made on history. A 1 MW / 2 MWh battery (95% each way, £5/MWh wear), GBP per MW-year, last week's prices / perfect foresight (actual: the whole year; model: 358 or 359 days, from the second week):

Year Actual Links Links + UC, marginal Links + UC, start 2023 36,362 / 46,440 1,604 / 9,275 10,982 / 25,701 4,228 / 15,228 2024 29,048 / 39,304 1,643 / 9,234 9,282 / 25,553 4,425 / 15,308 2025 36,208 / 44,974 648 / 9,728 11,293 / 26,038 4,384 / 15,723

With perfect foresight the model gives 55% to 65% of the actual value; planning on last week's prices, 30% to 32%.

A hurdle (hurdle_gbp_per_mwh) is still available but left at 0.

docs.title: FES pathways
docs.text:
system.fes scales the weather year's system by the ratio of the FES year to the weather year in the same pathway, so every half-hour keeps its weather and demand shape:

Weather-year input Scaled by FES (target year / weather year) Wind (transmission and embedded) Offshore Wind + Onshore Wind capacity Solar Solar PV capacity Nuclear, hydro Nuclear; Hydro capacity Biomass Biomass + CCS Biomass capacity CCGT and peaking capacity (DUKES) Gas + CCS Gas + Hydrogen capacity Coal none (set to 0) Demand ED1 annual system demand Interconnector capacity Interconnectors capacity Batteries added in full: FES GW, hours = GWh / GW Long-duration storage added: FES increase over the weather year (GW, GWh)

Pumped storage keeps its historic output. Hydrogen and CCS gas plant are costed as gas, because there is no open cost data for them. The weather year has to be a year the FES edition covers: from 2024 for FES 2025, from 2025 for the Ten Year Outlook. Any scale or capacity_mw you set overrides the FES value.

docs.title: A secure system first
docs.text:
As FES's fleets stand, several pathways cannot meet demand through 2025's cold, still spell in January. GB buys capacity through the Capacity Market to a reliability standard of 3 hours' loss of load expectation a year (DESNZ), so since v6.0 a FES system is made secure first (fes.adequacy: secure, the default): the least firm peaking capacity, in 250 MW steps and costed as gas peaking plant, is added until hours with unserved energy are within fes.lole_hours (3). That is the "Firm added" column: 2.5 GW in Holistic Transition 2030; 6.25 to 9.25 GW in Holistic Transition, Electric Engagement and Hydrogen Evolution 2035; 0.25 GW in the Ten Year Outlook 2035; none elsewhere. A single weather year is one draw, not an expectation; the saturation study below averages two.

fes.adequacy: as_modelled keeps the fleet as FES gives it, as before v6.0. Then six cases leave demand unserved, and the price sits at the £6,000/MWh value of lost load for much of it. Mean £/MWh and unserved GWh (hours with unserved energy), as modelled:

Pathway and year Links as fitted (default) availability: gap Every link at full capacity Holistic Transition 2030 85.0, 68.0 (16) 80.2, 47.0 (14) 66.2, 0 Holistic Transition 2035 210.5, 715.2 (81) 161.6, 508.0 (60) 84.9, 50.5 (8) Electric Engagement 2030 69.8, 9.7 (2) 60.1, 0 63.4, 0 Electric Engagement 2035 186.9, 683.2 (81) 150.5, 480.4 (60) 77.6, 10.9 (3) Hydrogen Evolution 2035 119.9, 214.8 (30) 93.9, 150.1 (22) 64.1, 0 Ten Year Outlook 2035 85.6, 17.1 (5) 58.5, 0 62.0, 0

The cause is link availability. The fitted availability holds on GB's tightest days in the record: on the 1% of days with the highest GB price in 2019–2025, links imported 3% (ElecLink) to 42% (Nemo Link, BritNed) of their capacity, below their fitted shares for every link but East West (39% against 38%), because neighbours were often short at the same time. So derating links at stress is supported by the flows. What the model leaves out is what FES counts on in those hours: demand response, new flexibility and neighbours' own 2030s fleets. The secure top-up stands in for all of that with the cheapest firm capacity, so read it as "this much firm capacity, or its equivalent", not as a forecast of new gas plant.

docs.title: A battery on pathway prices
docs.text:
The same 1 MW / 2 MWh battery (95% each way, £5/MWh wear) on 358 days of each modelled year (the first week has no last week to plan on), from the app's precomputed results (data/app/), GBP per MW-year:

Prices Last week's prices Perfect foresight Actual 2025 36,208 44,974 Model 2025, links + commitment 11,293 26,038 Holistic Transition 2030 / 2035 3,448 / 8,440 19,657 / 25,450 Electric Engagement 2030 / 2035 4,025 / 11,010 26,685 / 20,663 Hydrogen Evolution 2030 / 2035 5,860 / 5,145 17,514 / 22,031 Falling Behind 2030 / 2035 3,646 / 4,098 11,514 / 15,822 Ten Year Forecast 2030 / 2035 3,157 / 3,078 12,940 / 12,421 Ten Year Outlook 2030 / 2035 2,166 / 3,937 9,288 / 19,400

Compare pathways with the model's own 2025, not with actual 2025: on modelled 2025 prices the battery's perfect-foresight value is 58% of its actual value, and the model's daily spread is 76% of the real one. Against that baseline, every pathway's perfect-foresight value is about the same or lower: 2% lower in Holistic Transition 2035 and 2% higher in Electric Engagement 2030, 15% to 33% lower in Holistic Transition 2030, Electric Engagement and Hydrogen Evolution 2035, Hydrogen Evolution 2030 and the Ten Year Outlook 2035, and 39% to 64% lower in Falling Behind, the Ten Year Forecast and the Ten Year Outlook 2030. With secure systems the 2035 pathways no longer rise far above the baseline on days of lost load (before v6.0 they reached 1.8 to 2.7 times it), but scarcity still matters: with perfect foresight over the full year, the one or two days with an hour at £1,000/MWh or more earn 29% to 49% of the value in the six cases that have them (49% of Holistic Transition 2035's). Planning on last week's prices keeps 15% to 53% of the perfect-foresight value, against 81% on actual 2025 prices and 43% on the model's own 2025.

docs.title: How much storage can GB use?
docs.text:
The batteries above join a fleet that FES has already sized: 23 to 33 GW of batteries in 2035 in FES 2025's pathways, storing 1.3 to 1.5 hours on average. What happens to the value of one more battery as that fleet grows, once the system is secure? openenergy system saturation scales each pathway's 2035 battery fleet from none to three times FES's figure (same duration), and for each fleet adds the least firm capacity that keeps loss of load, averaged over the 2024 and 2025 weather years, within the 3-hour standard. A 1 MW / 2 MWh battery (95% each way, £5/MWh wear) is then valued with perfect foresight on each year's modelled prices (data/scenarios/saturation.csv; try it in the web app). FES 2025 publishes figures from 2024, so these two weather years are all a FES system can be scaled from today; the Ten Year Outlook, which has no 2024 wind, is left out.

The pathways with no shortfall once they have batteries first (Ten Year Forecast needs 0.75 GW of firm capacity with no batteries, none with half its fleet). GBP per MW-year, mean of the two weather years:

Battery fleet (× FES 2035) 0 0.5 1 2 3 Falling Behind: fleet GW 0 11.3 22.7 45.3 68.0 Falling Behind: one more battery earns 43,609 21,840 15,551 10,362 8,017 Falling Behind: daily spread (£/MWh) 72.2 47.9 40.6 32.6 28.2 Ten Year Forecast: fleet GW 0 15.0 29.9 59.9 89.8 Ten Year Forecast: one more battery earns 40,897 17,196 12,057 8,130 6,296 Ten Year Forecast: daily spread (£/MWh) 71.9 41.0 34.3 28.1 24.3

The first half of the FES fleet takes half or more of a battery's value away; the next two and a half fleets take nearly two thirds of what is left. Batteries earn by flattening the daily spread, so each one leaves less spread for the next. The two weather years agree: in Falling Behind a battery joining the FES fleet earns £14,927 on 2024's weather and £16,176 on 2025's.

The other three pathways are short of firm capacity in a cold, still spell, and the batteries do little about it:

Pathway Firm capacity added (GW) for a fleet of × 0 / 0.5 / 1 / 2 / 3 Firm capacity each MW of the FES fleet replaces (MW) Holistic Transition 11.25 / 9.25 / 8.25 / 8.0 / 8.25 0.10 Electric Engagement 11.25 / 8.75 / 8.25 / 7.25 / 7.25 0.09 Hydrogen Evolution 8.75 / 6.75 / 4.75 / 4.0 / 3.0 0.16

The FES fleets store under an hour and a half on average, and the shortfalls they would cover last longer: the first half of the fleet saves 2.0 to 2.5 GW of firm capacity, and the next two and a half fleets 1.0 to 3.75 GW more. In 250 MW steps the search is not perfectly monotonic (Holistic Transition needs 8.0 GW at twice the fleet and 8.25 GW at three times). In these pathways a battery's value also rests on a handful of scarcity days: a 1 MW battery with the FES fleet earns £16,591 in Holistic Transition, £17,441 in Electric Engagement and £26,961 in Hydrogen Evolution, of which 23%, 17% and 45% comes on the days with an hour priced at £1,000/MWh or more (one to three across the two weather years). Holistic Transition's and Electric Engagement's are all in 2025's weather; a value resting on them is a statement about one cold week, not about the pathway.

What this says, with its limits: in a GB system that has enough firm capacity, battery value halves or more as the first 11 to 15 GW of FES's fleet arrives, and falls to 15–18% of the first battery's value at three times the fleet. It is the perfect-foresight value of a 2-hour battery on a model whose daily spread is 76% of the real one in 2025, so the levels are lower bounds on what the spread allows and upper bounds on what a forecast captures; the shape of the curve is the result.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• One GB bus: no constraint between Scotland and England, which is where much FES curtailment happens.
  • Links take the neighbours' actual prices for the weather year, so neighbours do not respond to GB, and their 2030s fleets are not modelled. New links are not added as new neighbours; FES interconnector growth scales the existing ten.
  • Capacities from the register are today's; earlier limits on Moyle, IFA and BritNed are not modelled separately, only through each link's fitted availability (see Data).
  • Each link's availability is one number per direction for every hour and year (with availability: gap, one per price-gap bin); new FES capacity gets the existing links' shares.
  • Ember gives one price for Norway and one for Denmark; GB's links land in southern Norway and western Denmark.
  • The weather year's fuel and carbon prices are kept; storage efficiencies for FES batteries and long-duration storage are stated assumptions.
  • With unit commitment (the published scenarios), storage is planned one day at a time seeing 24 hours ahead; without it, with perfect foresight over the year.
