docs.title: Real batteries
docs.text: OpenEnergy's optimiser plans a hypothetical battery. This page checks it against what GB's real grid batteries did, unit by unit, from Elexon's open data (data/fleet/, written by scripts/fetch_fleet.py and compared by scripts/real_batteries.py). Try it in the web app.

docs.title: What open data shows about a battery
docs.text:
Elexon publishes, for every Balancing Mechanism (BM) unit:

  • its physical notification (PN): the position it expects to run at, fixed an hour ahead, which reflects every trade it made up to then but not where or at what price;
  • its metered output (B1610): what the meter recorded each half-hour;
  • the BM actions NESO took on it after that, with indicative volumes and cashflows.

What a battery is paid for frequency response, and the prices of its own trades, are not public unit by unit. So two measures are reported:

  1. Metered energy at the day-ahead price: what the unit physically did, valued at the GB day-ahead price. It compares directly with OpenEnergy's optimiser, which trades physical energy at that price.
  2. Estimated total: the unit's settlement as the market computes it, with one assumption. A unit is paid for its contracted position (taken as its PN, priced here at the day-ahead price because its real contract prices are unknown), for its BM actions, and for the difference between its meter and both, at the system (imbalance) price.

A PN is not what happened. One unit in the week of 20 January 2025 notified 1,262 MWh of exports and 443 MWh of imports and metered 615 and 723: it sold ahead and was then instructed back in the BM. Physical operation here always comes from the meter.

Battery units are found by name in Elexon's register (83 units; "battery", "BESS", "energy storage"); 78 of them ran between January 2021 and October 2026. Their registered capacity covers about half of GB's grid batteries by 2025 (REPD): the rest are not BM units or are not named as batteries. Units with no registered generation capacity use their demand capacity or metered peak.

docs.title: The fleet, year by year
docs.text:
Per MW-year of registered capacity, over the days each unit ran; the model is a 1 MW battery, 95% each way, £5/MWh wear, on the day-ahead market only:

Year Units MW-years (REPD battery MW) Full-power hours discharged Metered energy at day-ahead price Estimated total Model 1 h: last week's prices / OpenEnergy forecast / perfect Model 2 h: perfect 2023 32 969 (2,837) 306 £4,138 £9,532 £19,776 / £21,092 / £25,394 £46,440 2024 43 1,438 (3,504) 400 £4,056 £16,237 £15,619 / £17,897 / £21,459 £39,412 2025 55 2,066 (4,220) 402 £3,587 £16,699 £19,080 / £21,112 / £24,192 £44,974

The estimated total is made of (2025, per MW-year): contracts at the day-ahead price £17,673, BM actions £10,536 and imbalance −£11,511. Energy out per energy in at the meter was 82–85%.

2021 and 2022 are in the data but not the table: fewer than 20 units ran, under a quarter of the fleet, and they metered 67–69% of what they imported, as frequency response, which these files do not price, held their charge.

What it shows:

  • Real batteries do much less day-ahead arbitrage than the model. The energy they physically moved was worth £3,600–4,100 per MW-year at the day-ahead price, 17–23% of what a 1-hour battery planning on OpenEnergy's forecast earns there. They discharge as much (about 400 full-power hours a year since 2024) but not only at the day's peaks.
  • The shape is the same, a fifth the size. In 2025 the fleet charged most at 02:00–03:00 and 13:00 UTC and exported most at 17:00–18:00 (0.12–0.13 MW per MW running), the hours a 2-hour optimiser with perfect foresight uses (0.57–0.64 MW per MW). The fleet's net output correlates 0.34–0.42 with the day-ahead price from 2023 (data/fleet/hour_profile.csv).
  • Their money comes from elsewhere. On the estimate, real batteries made £16,200–16,700 per MW-year in 2024 and 2025: 69–76% of what a 1-hour optimiser with perfect foresight earns on the day-ahead market, and 79–91% of what it earns on OpenEnergy's forecast, through the BM, intraday trading and positions that are bought back, plus frequency response, which is not in these figures.

docs.title: North and south of the border
docs.text:
Year Zone Units Estimated total Contracts at day-ahead BM actions Imbalance Metered energy at day-ahead 2024 Scotland 8 £17,148 £34,167 £3,574 −£20,593 £5,896 2024 England and Wales 35 £15,990 £14,582 £9,680 −£8,272 £3,559 2025 Scotland 11 £17,578 £43,736 −£2,809 −£23,349 £5,423 2025 England and Wales 44 £16,502 £11,845 £13,520 −£8,863 £3,177

GBP per MW-year. Transmission-connected units are placed by their transmission loss factor, which is set by zone. Scottish batteries end up with about the same total by a different route: they sell far more ahead and are then paid less, or pay, in the BM and imbalance, where NESO buys power back north of the B6 boundary that the lines south cannot carry. They also discharged more (448–491 full-power hours against 383–387), and their metered energy was worth more at the day-ahead price. A location's value shows up in how a battery is paid, not (yet) in how much.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Frequency response (Dynamic Containment and its successors) is not in these figures, so real revenue is understated, by most in 2021–2023 when response paid most.
  • The estimate prices contracts at the day-ahead price; batteries that sold intraday at better prices earned more than shown, and the imbalance term absorbs the difference.
  • BM cashflows are Elexon's indicative values, not final settlement.
  • Battery duration is not registered, so the comparison shows 1-hour and 2-hour models.
  • Units are found by name, checked by hand once; a battery named otherwise is missed.

Data: Elexon BMRS (BMRS data licence; contains BMRS data © Elexon Limited copyright and database right 2026), Ember and Elexon prices as bundled. Details in data/fleet/README.md.

docs.title: Reports
docs.text:
openenergy report turns saved outputs into one HTML file of charts and tables. It reads what the other commands wrote, so nothing is re-run and any past run can be reported.

uv sync --extra report      # or: pip install 'openenergy[report]'  (plotly)
uv run openenergy run examples/gb-2019-naive.yaml --out outputs/naive
uv run openenergy run examples/gb-2019-perfect.yaml --out outputs/perfect
uv run openenergy report outputs/naive outputs/perfect -o outputs/report.html

See the example report for GB 2019 (a battery on real prices and the system model), built from the bundled data when these docs are built.

docs.title: What goes in
docs.text:
Input Written by Sections A run directory openenergy run Key figures; cumulative revenue against perfect foresight; revenue by month; average day; stored energy by day and hour; price and forecast; forecast error by hour; revenue by market, plant output and emissions where the run has them A system directory openenergy system run Key figures; generation by month; price duration curve; mean price by hour; curtailment and emissions by month; battery figures when present A backcast directory openenergy system validate --out The per-year table; model and actual price by hour and by month; duration curves; gas and coal by year A sweep CSV openenergy sweep --out Results table; ranking; revenue per MW-year against each swept setting

The kind is detected from the files. Several run directories also get a comparison section (key figures side by side and cumulative revenue on one chart), as do several system directories (duration curves and price by hour together).

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
Option Default Meaning -o, --out report.html File to write --title OpenEnergy report Title at the top of the page --cdn off Load plotly.js from its CDN: about 0.4 MB per chart instead of a 5 MB self-contained file, but the report then needs internet to show charts

By default the report is self-contained and opens offline. Charts are interactive: zoom, pan, hide a series by clicking its legend entry, or save a chart as PNG from its toolbar.

docs.title: Numbers and sources
docs.text: Key figures come from each run's summary.json exactly as written, so they match what the command printed. Each section repeats the run's notes and data attribution, and the footer states the licences; share the report with those intact. openenergy run also writes benchmark_daily.csv, the perfect-foresight benchmark by day, which the revenue chart uses.

docs.title: In Python
docs.text:
The charts are plain functions from pandas to plotly figures, so they work in notebooks and apps too:

from openenergy.report import build_report, load_output
from openenergy.report import figures

run = load_output("outputs/naive")
figures.state_of_charge(run.intervals).show()
html = build_report([run], title="Naive 2019")

docs.title: Research with the Python API
docs.text: Every step of a scenario is a plain function, so experiments that do not fit a YAML file are a few lines of Python.

docs.title: How much is a better forecast worth?
docs.text:
examples/forecast_error_sweep.py adds Gaussian error of increasing size to the actual 2019 GB prices and measures the share of perfect-foresight revenue a 1 MW / 2 MWh battery keeps:

raw = OPSDCsvSource(DATA).prices("GB_GBN", date(2019, 1, 1), date(2019, 12, 31))
prices, _ = fill_gaps(raw, max_gap_hours=2)
battery = BatterySpec(power_mw=1, energy_mwh=2)
config = BacktestConfig(dispatch=DispatchConfig(degradation_cost=5))
benchmark = run_backtest(battery, prices, PerfectForesight(prices), config)

for error_std in (0.0, 2.0, 5.0, 10.0, 20.0):
    forecaster = NoisyForesight(prices, error_std=error_std, seed=1)
    summary = summarise(run_backtest(battery, prices, forecaster, config), benchmark)
Error std (GBP/MWh) Revenue (GBP) Capture Cycles 0 19,235 100.0% 468 2 18,846 98.0% 494 5 17,261 89.7% 602 10 10,626 55.2% 903 20 −164 −0.9% 1,309

Beyond about £5/MWh of error the optimiser starts trading noise: cycles double and revenue collapses. The noise here is independent hour to hour, which is harsher than real forecast errors; a correlated error model is a natural next experiment.

docs.title: How good is OpenEnergy's forecast?
docs.text:
The fundamentals forecaster (v6.0, Concepts) plans each day at noon the day before on what was published by then: NESO's day-ahead demand forecast, Elexon's day-ahead wind forecast, the daily gas price and the prices of every auction that had cleared. A new model is trained each month on everything known before the month began. examples/fundamentals_forecast.py backtests a 1 MW / 2 MWh battery (95% each way, £5/MWh wear in the plan) on Ember's GB prices with it and with last week's prices (2026 to 28 October):

Year Perfect foresight (£) Last week's prices (£) Capture MAE (£/MWh) OpenEnergy forecast (£) Capture MAE (£/MWh) 2019 19,702 14,074 71.4% 6.1 15,281 77.6% 3.9 2020 22,623 17,362 76.7% 7.7 18,607 82.2% 4.6 2021 90,264 75,065 83.2% 31.3 71,665 79.4% 26.3 2022 103,705 77,954 75.2% 61.4 81,135 78.2% 33.9 2023 46,440 36,362 78.3% 20.0 39,840 85.8% 11.8 2024 39,412 29,128 73.9% 19.5 33,894 86.0% 9.3 2025 44,974 36,208 80.5% 21.8 39,745 88.4% 10.6 2026 41,424 32,838 79.3% 27.7 36,827 88.9% 14.3

What this shows:

  • The error roughly halves, the revenue gap closes by a third to a half. From 2023 the forecast's mean absolute error is 48–59% of last week's, and the battery keeps 86–89% of the perfect-foresight revenue instead of 74–81%. A battery is paid for the day's shape, not its level, so a smaller error buys less revenue than it seems to.
  • 2021 is the exception. Gas prices rose through 2021 faster than a model trained on the calmer years before each month could follow; last week's prices carried the new level with them and kept 83.2% against 79.4%. By 2022 the forecast was ahead again.
  • A plain model forecasts too flat a day. Each month the forecast's shape around its mean is stretched by 1, 1.25, 1.5, 1.75 or 2, whichever would have earned a reference battery most over the previous 90 days (past data only). It chose 1 in 64 of the 94 months, 1.25 in 24 and 1.5 in 6.
  • Planning one day ahead still pays. With dispatch.lookahead_days: 1 on examples/gb-2022-naive.yaml's battery, the forecast earns 5.0% (2021) to 13.4% (2019) more.

The bundled forecast (data/forecasts/) is exactly what a backtest with forecast: fundamentals computes, so forecast: {method: fundamentals, path: ...} gives the same results without training (a test checks a week of it against a live run). What the forecast may know is tested too: a later wind forecast or a price after the decision time changes nothing.

docs.title: Can reinforcement learning do better?
docs.text:
A reinforcement-learning agent can learn to trade directly, without a forecast and an optimiser. In the v6.0 design work an agent (PPO, Stable-Baselines3, 0.4 and 3 million steps) saw exactly what the optimiser sees at noon the day before: an earlier version of OpenEnergy's forecast for the day, the hour and the energy stored. Trained on 2021–2023 and tested on 2024–2026, it kept 27–38% of the perfect-foresight revenue; the optimiser planning on the same forecast kept 78–83%. More training did not close the gap. The optimiser solves the day exactly; the agent has to rediscover that, from noisy rewards.

So OpenEnergy keeps "forecast, then optimise", and ships the test as an environment for anyone who wants to try (pip install 'openenergy[rl]', Gymnasium):

from openenergy.rl import BatteryTradingEnv, episodes, optimiser_baseline, policy_revenue

days = episodes(prices, NaiveLastWeek(), dates)  # forecasts as the backtest makes them
env = BatteryTradingEnv(days, BatterySpec(power_mw=1, energy_mwh=2), wear=5.0)
baseline = optimiser_baseline(days, env.battery)  # GBP per day, the bar to beat
mine = policy_revenue(env, lambda observation: agent(observation))

Each episode is a day: the action is the share of power to sell (positive) or buy, the reward is the hour's revenue at the actual price less wear, and ending the day away from the starting energy is settled at the day's mean price plus £20/MWh. A policy that replays the optimiser's plan earns exactly the baseline (tested).

docs.title: Do solar and wind earn the average price?
docs.text:
openenergy capture compares what each technology earned per MWh with the plain average price, per year:

Year Solar capture rate Wind capture rate 2015 105.9% 96.4% 2016 94.2% 96.3% 2017 93.8% 99.5% 2018 98.3% 99.2% 2019 96.1% 98.1%

In GB day-ahead prices up to 2019, neither technology was heavily cannibalised: both earned within about 6% of baseload, and almost no output fell in negative-price hours (GB had only 81 such hours in the whole extract). Solar's 2015 premium reflects output coinciding with daytime peaks. OPSD's solar capacity factors run high because reported capacity lags new build (see Data), which affects capacity factor but not capture rate.

docs.title: How big should a shared connection be?
docs.text:
examples/colocation_grid_sweep.py puts 10 MW of solar and a 5 MW / 10 MWh battery behind one connection of increasing size and compares each with the same assets on separate connections (15 MW in total), for GB 2019 with last week's prices:

Shared limit (MW) Site (GBP) Separate (GBP) Difference 5.0 590,314 618,256 −27,942 7.0 615,787 618,256 −2,469 10.0 618,093 618,256 −163 12.5 618,243 618,256 −13 15.0 618,244 618,256 −12

A battery added behind the solar farm's own 10 MW connection gives up only £163 a year: solar output and battery discharge rarely need the connection at the same time. From 12.5 MW the gap (£12–13, two parts in 100,000) is within the solver's tolerance. Shrinking the shared connection below the plant's capacity starts to cost real money, so the saving on connection capacity has to exceed these figures. Plans use actual solar output, so these are upper bounds.

docs.title: Is planning under price uncertainty worth it?
docs.text:
examples/stochastic_value.py plans each day at noon the day before in four ways and settles every plan at actual GB prices (Ember). The scenarios are last week's prices plus each of that forecast's daily errors over the last 28 days. Revenue is after a £5/MWh wear cost, for a 1 MW / 2 MWh battery:

Year Plan Revenue (£) vs forecast Loss days 2019 One forecast (last week) 4,640 82 2019 Scenario mean (risk-neutral) 4,315 −7.0% 90 2019 Half CVaR (worst 10%) 3,412 −26.5% 78 2019 Full CVaR 2,221 −52.1% 63 2019 One forecast, one day lookahead 6,391 +37.7% 83 2022 One forecast 64,610 9 2022 Scenario mean 62,100 −3.9% 12 2022 Half CVaR 50,311 −22.1% 34 2022 Full CVaR 40,613 −37.1% 40 2022 One forecast, one day lookahead 71,213 +10.2% 43 2024 One forecast 17,642 34 2024 Scenario mean 16,927 −4.1% 45 2024 Half CVaR 12,163 −31.1% 43 2024 Full CVaR 8,873 −49.7% 44 2024 One forecast, one day lookahead 21,171 +20.1% 46

What this shows:

  • A risk-neutral scenario plan is just another forecast. The plan is fixed before prices clear and paid at actual prices, so revenue is linear in price: the expected revenue of any plan is its revenue at the mean scenario, and the best plan over the scenarios is the best plan for their mean. These scenarios shift last week's prices by their recent average error, which made the forecast slightly worse every year. With only a day-ahead market, the value of the stochastic solution is zero by construction. A prototype that also re-planned the next day per scenario (two-stage, not part of the example) gained under £1 a year over the same two-day plan on the mean scenario.
  • Risk aversion costs revenue and does not reliably cut bad days. Weighting the worst 10% of scenarios (CVaR) loses 22–52% of revenue; in 2022 it more than tripled the days with a loss.
  • A longer horizon pays. Planning today with tomorrow's forecast, rather than returning to the same charge every midnight, adds 10–38% after wear cost. Loss days rise because a day that fills the battery for tomorrow books the cost today and the revenue tomorrow.

The lookahead across all years, with examples/gb-2022-naive.yaml (last week's prices, £5/MWh wear cost in the plan) and dispatch.lookahead_days set; revenue per MW-year before wear cost, perfect foresight with the same lookahead:

Year Revenue, 0 days 1 day Change Capture, 0 days 1 day Cycles, 0 days 1 day 2017 20,633 22,326 +8.2% 78.6% 80.5% 526 524 2018 18,887 20,557 +8.8% 74.4% 76.5% 529 526 2019 13,943 15,818 +13.4% 71.4% 74.7% 468 474 2020 17,144 19,669 +14.7% 76.7% 80.5% 419 428 2021 74,169 78,259 +5.5% 83.1% 84.8% 620 600 2022 76,948 82,938 +7.8% 75.0% 76.8% 661 627 2023 35,957 40,093 +11.5% 78.2% 81.5% 612 585 2024 28,690 31,860 +11.0% 73.8% 76.8% 569 551 2025 35,861 38,937 +8.6% 80.5% 82.7% 571 547

One day of lookahead adds 5.5–14.7% revenue every year, and from 2021 does so with fewer cycles. Two or three days change revenue by under £20 a year: last week's prices say little about the day after tomorrow.

Uncertainty could matter when a later decision can react to prices, such as balancing or frequency response. Revenue stacking checks both: response availability is also committed before its price is known, so the same argument applies; balancing does give the battery a later decision, but without an imbalance-price forecast, which open data does not provide, it gains in some years and loses in others. The lookahead is a scenario setting, dispatch.lookahead_days.

docs.text:

docs.title: Revenue stacking
docs.text: A GB battery can sell more than day-ahead trading. OpenEnergy v3.5 adds the frequency response services NESO buys every day, co-optimised with trading in the same plan, and measures what the imbalance (balancing) price is worth with the information open data gives.

docs.title: Frequency response
docs.text:
NESO buys three dynamic response services, each in a low direction (export when frequency falls) and a high direction (import when it rises), by day-ahead auction in four-hour EFA blocks:

Service Codes Responds Energy held Dynamic Containment DCL, DCH mostly beyond ±0.2 Hz, after a fault 15 minutes Dynamic Moderation DML, DMH mostly beyond ±0.1 Hz 30 minutes Dynamic Regulation DRL, DRH continuously beyond ±0.015 Hz 60 minutes

Add a response section to a battery scenario (reference):

response:
  path: ../data/response/gb_dynamic_response.csv
  services: [DCL, DCH]

uv run openenergy run examples/gb-2025-stacked.yaml

docs.title: How it is modelled
docs.text:
Each day is planned at the usual decision time (noon the day before) as one optimisation over trading and response:

  • MW per block. For every block and service the plan chooses MW held, constant across the block. Blocks that run past midnight are fixed by the day they start in and carried into the next day's plan.
  • Power. MW held for low services plus net discharge cannot exceed the power rating; likewise for high services and net charge. MW contracted in each direction is at most the power rating.
  • Energy. The battery keeps enough stored energy (or room) to deliver each service for its full duration at every point in the block, and, for a block that runs past the horizon, to stay idle until it ends.
  • Utilisation. Responding moves energy. OpenEnergy uses the monthly average delivery per MW from NESO's one-second frequency data and the service delivery envelopes (DC about 0.007, DM 0.03–0.04, DR 0.13–0.14 MWh per MW per hour in 2024–2025). That energy changes the stored energy, counts towards cycles, ageing and the wear cost, and by default is unpaid: under NESO's ABSVD adjustment a balancing-mechanism battery is neither charged for energy it imports in high services nor paid for energy it exports in low services (NESO, Dynamic Response A18 Submission Document, 2025). energy: day_ahead buys and sells it at the trading price instead.
  • Prices. MW held is paid the actual clearing price (GBP per MW per hour). The plan uses forecast: previous_day: the latest earlier block at the same UK clock time whose auction result was public at the decision time (results are assumed public at 15:00 UK time the day before the EFA day). actual plans on the clearing price itself, an upper bound, and is what the perfect-foresight benchmark uses.

Left out, and stated in summary.json: the battery is a price-taker whose offers are always accepted at the clearing price; it is always available and never penalised for performance; delivery follows the monthly average rather than the frequency on the day; reserve products (balancing, quick and slow reserve) and the Balancing Mechanism are not modelled.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
examples/gb-2025-stacked.yaml for each year and service set (1 MW / 2 MWh, 95% each way, last week's day-ahead prices, £5/MWh wear cost in the plan); revenue per MW-year before wear cost, as openenergy run reports it:

Year Day-ahead only + DC + DC, DM + DC, DM, DR 2022 76,948 197,081 217,004 395,148 2023 35,957 61,907 72,392 112,437 2024 28,690 45,226 47,443 51,210 2025 35,861 63,872 75,766 90,766

With utilisation energy bought and sold at the day-ahead price (energy: day_ahead):

Year + DC + DC, DM + DC, DM, DR 2022 198,119 202,931 267,469 2023 61,787 68,775 112,425 2024 45,026 56,826 79,948 2025 63,788 83,106 125,634

DM and DR start on 26 March 2022, so their 2022 columns cover 281 days, scaled to a year.

What this shows:

  • Dynamic Containment is the robust gain. Adding DC raises revenue by 58–156% every year, and the answer barely moves with how utilisation energy is settled (DC is rarely called). DC availability is 60–77% of the stacked revenue.
  • The battery works less for more. With DC, equivalent cycles fall from 569–661 a year to 319–393: holding power for DC pays more than the marginal arbitrage it displaces.
  • DM and DR depend on an assumption. DR moves 0.13–0.14 MWh per MW per hour, so who pays for that energy decides its value: in 2024 adding DR to DC and DM adds 8% when the energy is free and 41% when it is bought and sold at the day-ahead price. The default (free) follows NESO's ABSVD treatment of balancing-mechanism units; NESO's 2025 A18 document describes non-BM units as exposed to imbalance prices on it instead, and proposes to extend ABSVD to them.
  • Thin markets. DR low cleared a median 9 MW per block in 2022 and about 480 MW in 2025, against about 1,100–1,250 MW of DC; a price-taker result for one small battery says nothing about what a fleet entering these markets would earn.
  • Prices fell, then partly recovered. DC low cleared at £19.20/MW/h on average in 2022 and £2.25 in 2024, then £3.93 in 2025 (see data/response/README.md).

docs.title: Balancing
docs.text:
GB's imbalance price (the system price, one per half-hour since 2015) settles any difference between a battery's contracted position and what it delivers. It is the obvious "later market": a battery could take a day-ahead position and then deviate when the imbalance price looks better. examples/imbalance_value.py tests this on Elexon's system prices, 2016 to October 2026 (data/balancing/), after a £5/MWh wear cost:

Year Days Follow day-ahead Perfect imbalance foresight Re-plan each half-hour (t−2 price) Re-plan on known day-ahead Imbalance only 2019 355 4,421 53,609 5,216 9,210 −373 2022 361 64,275 328,633 75,099 83,074 37,981 2024 366 17,642 101,567 17,816 23,548 11,277 2025 365 24,693 106,912 21,652 31,091 10,486

Days with a missing price in either market are left out.

What this shows:

  • The upside is large. Knowing the day's imbalance prices would earn 4–12 times the day-ahead revenue: the price is far more volatile than day-ahead.
  • A simple real-time strategy is a gamble. Re-planning before each half-hour on the latest published price (two periods back) earns 18% and 17% more than just delivering the day-ahead position in 2019 and 2022, 1% more in 2024 and 12% less in 2025. Trading imbalance alone on the same information earns 42–64% of day-ahead from 2022 and lost money in 2019. The value is in forecasting the imbalance price, which open data does not give.
  • Re-planning on known day-ahead prices gains 26–108%, but that is the value of knowing the day-ahead price (a battery bidding a curve into the auction captures much of it), not of balancing.

Before v6.0 a re-plan could end each horizon fuller than it began, which pushed every later target up; with that fixed, the half-hourly re-plan went from losing 6–39% to the mixed result above. OpenEnergy still does not offer a balancing mode: a strategy that gains in some years and loses in others on the information available would mislead.

docs.title: Planning under uncertainty
docs.text: v3.3 showed that for day-ahead trading a plan over price scenarios equals a plan on their mean. The same holds for frequency response: MW is committed before the auction clears and paid the clearing price, so revenue is linear in price and the value of a stochastic solution is zero. Balancing is the one market with a genuine later decision, and above, without a forecast of the imbalance price, it gains in some years and loses in others. Stochastic planning therefore stays out of OpenEnergy until a later market with an open, forecastable price is added.

docs.title: Scenarios
docs.text:
A scenario is a YAML file describing the data, the battery, the forecast and the dispatch settings. Unknown keys and invalid values are rejected with the setting named.

  path: ../data/time_series/time_series_60min_singleindex_filtered.csv
  zone: GB_GBN
  start: 2019-01-01
  end: 2019-12-31
battery:
  power_mw: 1
  energy_mwh: 2
  eta_charge: 0.95
  eta_discharge: 0.95
  cycle_fade: 0.00002
  calendar_fade: 0.01
forecast: naive_last_week

  degradation_cost: 5

docs.title: System scenarios
docs.text: A file with a system: section instead of data: describes one GB year for the system model: scaled renewables and fixed profiles, thermal capacity, fuel and carbon prices, added storage, and optionally a battery valued on the modelled prices. Run it with openenergy system run; the full reference is on that page.

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
openenergy run writes to outputs/<name>/ unless --out is given:

  • intervals.csv: price, forecast, charge, discharge, stored energy and revenue per interval; sites add available output, plant to grid, plant to battery, curtailment, grid charging, net export and premium;
  • daily.csv: revenue, expected revenue, energy charged and discharged, cycles, SOH and end-of-day energy; sites add premium, available and curtailed energy;
  • benchmark_daily.csv: the same daily columns for the perfect-foresight benchmark, when the scenario is not perfect foresight itself;
  • summary.json: the headline metrics, skipped days with reasons, the number of interpolated intervals, the full validated configuration, the package version and the data attribution; sites add the co-location comparison, the plant's capture metrics, the number of clipped capacity factors and the upper-bound note; carbon runs add emissions_t, the NESO attribution, rejected intensity values and the average-intensity caveat; response runs add response_revenue, the NESO attribution and a note on what the response model leaves out.

With response, intervals.csv and daily.csv also hold energy_revenue and response_revenue (their sum is revenue), and intervals.csv the MW held for each service (dcl_mw, ...).

openenergy report outputs/<name> turns these files into an HTML page of charts; see Reports.

docs.title: System model
docs.text:
The system model rebuilds the GB power system hour by hour from public data: which plants run, what that costs, and the price it implies. It first replays 2015–2020 and checks the result against what happened, then answers what-if questions on that tested base.

uv sync --extra system   # or: pip install 'openenergy[system]'  (PyPSA, for storage)
uv run openenergy system validate
uv run openenergy system run examples/gb-2019-system.yaml

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
GB is one bus. Each hour, demand must equal supply:

  • Demand is NESO's total generation for that hour.
  • Fixed at historic output: nuclear, biomass, hydro, imports, pumped storage and "other". There is no open data to model continental prices or plant-level constraints, so these follow history (scaled in scenarios).
  • Wind and solar are free to run and can be curtailed when supply exceeds demand.
  • Thermal plant (CCGT, coal, and gas turbines with oil engines as "peaking") runs in order of short-run marginal cost. Each group's capacity (DUKES, interpolated between year ends) is derated by availability and split into equal tranches whose efficiencies spread around the fleet average:
\[c_{k,t} = \frac{p_{f,q(t)} + s_{f,t} + \lambda_t\, e_f}{\eta_k} + v\]

with fuel price \(p\) (gas: the daily System Average Price from 2018, DESNZ's quarterly price paid by power producers before; coal and oil: quarterly, DESNZ), carbon price support \(s\) (HMRC), ETS price \(\lambda\) (EU ETS to 2020, UK ETS from 2021; one price per year from 1 April), emission factor \(e_f\) and efficiency \(\eta_k\). The price is the cost of the last unit needed, or the value of lost load (default £6,000/MWh) if capacity runs out.

Without storage every hour is independent, so the merit order is the exact least-cost dispatch. Added storage links hours together; then the model is solved as one linear programme per year with PyPSA and HiGHS. On 2019 data both give identical prices and costs, and a year with storage solves in under two seconds.

Assumption (default) Why 5 tranches per group; CCGT efficiency ±4 points, coal ±2 points around the DUKES average Real fleets mix old and new units Availability 0.9 Peak gas output is 80–89% of CCGT plus gas-turbine capacity each year Peaking plant costed as gas at 35% efficiency Gas turbines and oil engines rarely run Variable O&M 0 No open source; configurable

None of these is fitted to prices. Every one can be changed in a scenario's assumptions section.

Five tranches is enough: with links and unit commitment (2023–2025), the marginal price's mean moves by under £1/MWh and its daily spread by under 5% between 5, 10 and 20 CCGT tranches, while each step costs several times the solve time. More tranches only split ties, so fewer hours repeat the previous hour's price.

What the table shows:

  • Average prices are a little low every year. The yearly mean is £1.6–4.8/MWh below actual, and £4.5–4.8 below in each year from 2016. Fuel and carbon costs explain most of the price level. From 2018 the gas price is the daily wholesale price, which leaves out the network charges power stations pay; DESNZ's quarterly price paid includes them and contracts struck earlier, and put 2019 within £0.6 (below).
  • Peaks are missed every year. The 95th percentile is £10–20 below actual. A cost-only model has no scarcity pricing, start-up costs or bidding above cost, so its prices are much flatter than the market's (2019 standard deviation £6.9/MWh).
  • Coal left the model faster than it left the grid, except in 2018. In 2016, 2017, 2019 and 2020 the model runs about a third or less of the coal that actually ran (2019: 1.7 against 5.9 TWh). Once carbon price support made coal dearer than most gas, a pure cost ranking switches it off; real coal plants kept running for reasons outside a cost-only model. In 2015 the model runs more coal than happened.

These are the model's limits, reported rather than tuned away. Use it for direction and relative change between scenarios, not to forecast prices. Unit commitment addresses the flat prices; the coal gap remains.

docs.title: Unit commitment
docs.text:
Real plants cannot follow demand freely: starting a unit costs money and wear, and a running unit cannot go below a minimum stable output. So plants stay on overnight and sell below cost rather than restart, and recover start costs over short peak runs. With system.commitment: true (or system validate --commitment) the model includes this:

  • Each CCGT, coal and peaking tranche is a number of identical units \(n_{k,t}\) (whole numbers), each of size \(U\), with output between \(m U n_{k,t}\) and \(U n_{k,t}\) (and at most the tranche's available capacity).
  • Starting units costs \(C\,U \max(0, n_{k,t} - n_{k,t-1})\), added to fuel and carbon cost.
  • Each day is solved as a mixed-integer programme with HiGHS, seeing 24 hours beyond the day; units online and storage carry over to the next day.
  • Load is shed only when available capacity runs out, as in the merit order.
Technology Unit size \(U\) (MW) Minimum stable output \(m\) Start cost \(C\) (£/MW) CCGT 500 40% 34.29 Coal 500 18% 40.53 Peaking 40 25% 14.96

Unit size and minimum output are from the Danish Energy Agency's technology catalogue; start costs are NREL's median warm-start costs, converted from 2011 US dollars (see Data sources). They describe typical modern plant, not the GB fleet, and none is fitted to prices.

Two prices come out:

  • Marginal (price: marginal): the cost of one more MWh with the units online fixed. It ignores start costs, so it can sit below what a started unit needs.
  • Start (price: start): each run of a unit spreads its start cost over the energy it produces in that run; the hour's price is the higher of the marginal price and the highest such cost-plus-start of any unit running.

What the tables show:

  • Prices now move within the day. The daily spread rises from £2–4 to £11–25, and the 2019 standard deviation from £6.9 to £9.2 with the marginal price and £9.7 with the start price (actual £11.7). Real spreads are still larger every year, most of all in 2016 (£69), whose spikes the model does not produce.

docs.text:
The system data runs to the end of 2025, and Ember's prices cover the years after OPSD stops (see Data). The default backcast still ends in September 2020, so the tables above do not change; later years are one flag away:

uv run openenergy system validate --start 2021-01-01 --end 2025-12-31 [--commitment --price start]

Gas and coal TWh are from the merit order; unit commitment gives gas within 1 TWh of it.

What the table shows:

  • With the daily gas price the timing is right; the coal is not. The model's prices now follow the crisis (correlation 0.81 in 2022; 0.40 with quarterly gas, see above). At crisis gas prices the model's remaining coal plant is cheaper than gas, so in 2021 and 2022 it burns 15.2 and 19.8 TWh of coal where 5.0 and 4.3 ran, and 10–15 TWh less gas than actual. From 2023 gas output is within 2 TWh of actual.
  • Spikes are missed. In 2022 the actual 95th percentile is £415; the model reaches £298, or £307 with unit commitment. Daily spreads in 2021–2022 averaged £146–156; unit commitment gets £41–51.
  • From 2023 the mean is £3–12 above actual (merit order £3–8, start price £8–12), with correlation 0.53–0.67 and the 95th percentile within £15 of actual.

The cost-based model now explains the level and timing of prices through the gas crisis from fuel prices alone, but not the size of their daily swings. Read results for 2021–2022 as a lower bound on spreads.

docs.title: What if: more wind
docs.text:
The same 2019 weather and demand with wind output scaled (system.scale.wind):

Wind Price mean Price std Curtailed (TWh) Fossil CO2 (Mt) System cost (£m) ×1 38.04 6.92 0.0 44.8 4,518 ×2 28.87 16.71 7.9 25.8 2,638 ×3 20.11 19.20 38.7 15.6 1,614

Prices fall and spread out as more hours are set by free wind. Curtailment rises steeply because nuclear, imports and biomass are held at historic output: the fixed floor is the binding constraint, as in System analysis.

docs.title: What if: storage in a windy system
docs.text:
At three times 2019 wind, adding 4-hour storage (system.storage.<name>):

Storage Curtailed (TWh) Fossil CO2 (Mt) System cost (£m) none 38.7 15.6 1,614 5 GW 36.2 14.8 1,535 10 GW 34.4 14.2 1,478 20 GW 31.8 13.4 1,393

Each 5 GW recovers less curtailed wind than the one before. Storage here has perfect foresight over the year, so these are best cases.

docs.title: A battery on modelled prices
docs.text:
A system scenario can value a battery on its own modelled prices, with the same no-lookahead forecasts as on market data. For a 1 MW / 2 MWh battery (95% each way), revenue per MW-year:

Prices Last-week forecast Perfect foresight Real 2019 market 16,055 22,509 Model, 2019 −129 322 Model with unit commitment, 2019, marginal price 2,730 10,043 Model with unit commitment, 2019, start price 1,334 8,772 Model, wind ×3 1,137 11,943 Model, wind ×3 with 10 GW storage −505 5,331

On the merit-order 2019 prices a battery earns almost nothing: the cost-based price is too flat. With unit commitment the daily shape gives it £9–10k with perfect foresight, under half the real market's £22.5k; the rest came from spikes and bidding the model leaves out. With three times the wind, spreads open up and perfect-foresight value reaches £12k; 10 GW of other storage then cuts it by more than half. Forecasting on last week's prices fails on these spiky, weather-driven prices.

docs.title: What if: carbon price support
docs.text:
2016 with and without the GB carbon price support (system.carbon_price_support), at the 2016 EU ETS price and at £50/t:

Carbon price support EU ETS (£/t) Price mean Fossil CO2 (Mt) on 4.14 35.77 61.5 off 4.14 26.11 101.1 on 50 55.96 58.5 off 50 48.07 58.7

With a low EU price, the support decides whether coal or gas runs first. In this model it cut 2016 emissions by about 40 Mt and raised the average price by about £10/MWh. At £50/t the EU price alone puts coal behind gas and the support adds cost without cutting emissions. The backcast shows real coal fell more slowly than the model's, so treat the size of the effect as an upper bound.

docs.title: Scenario reference
docs.text:
name: gb-2019-wind3-storage
system:
  data: ../data/system                 # written by scripts/fetch_system_data.py
  prices:                              # optional: actual prices to compare, earlier files first
    - ../data/time_series/time_series_60min_singleindex_filtered.csv
    - ../data/prices/gb_day_ahead_ember.csv
  year: 2019                           # 2015 (from April) to 2025
  start: 2019-01-01                    # optional: a shorter window within the year
  end: 2019-03-31
  scale: {wind: 3.0, solar: 1.0}       # also nuclear, biomass, hydro, imports, other, pumped_storage
  capacity_mw: {coal: 0}               # replace installed ccgt, coal or peaking MW
  fuel_price_scale: {gas: 1.5}         # multiply gas or coal prices
  ets_gbp_per_t: 50                    # replace the ETS price (eu_ets_gbp_per_t also accepted)
  carbon_price_support: true
  storage:
    fleet: {power_mw: 10000, hours: 4, efficiency: 0.85}   # power_mw 0 leaves it out
  assumptions: {tranches: 5, availability: 0.9}
  voll: 6000
  backend: auto                        # auto, merit or pypsa
  commitment: false                    # true: start-up costs and minimum stable output
  lookahead_hours: 24                  # with commitment: hours seen beyond each day
  price: marginal                      # or start (needs commitment)
  interconnectors: fixed               # or links (from 2019; see Forward scenarios)
  fes: {pathway: Holistic Transition, year: 2035}   # optional, needs links
battery: {power_mw: 1, energy_mwh: 2}  # optional: value a battery on modelled prices
forecast: naive_last_week              # or perfect_foresight

interconnectors and fes are described in Forward scenarios.

Sweeps work on any setting, in the order given:

uv run openenergy sweep examples/gb-2019-system.yaml \
  --set system.scale.wind=1,2,3 --set system.storage.fleet.power_mw=0,10000 \
  --set system.storage.fleet.hours=4

openenergy system run writes dispatch.csv (hourly price, output by technology, storage, curtailment, emissions) and summary.json with the data attributions.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• One bus: no transmission constraints between Scotland and England.
  • Unit commitment is optional and simplified: no minimum up or down times, ramp limits or start fuel, typical rather than GB-specific unit data, and one day planned at a time.
  • Imports and other fixed profiles cannot respond to price, unless interconnectors are links (Forward scenarios), which take the neighbours' prices as given and trade up to each link's availability fitted from its flows. Links work with unit commitment from v4.2.
  • Gas is priced at the daily wholesale price from 2018 (without the network charges power stations pay) and the quarterly price paid before; coal and oil are quarterly; the ETS is one price per year (from 1 April).
  • Storage optimisation has perfect foresight over the year.
  • Emissions cover GB fossil plant only (no imports or biomass).

docs.title: System analysis
docs.text: OpenEnergy can also look at the whole GB system: how wind and solar reshape the demand left for other plant, when they produce more than the system can use, how much storage that calls for, and what storage does to emissions.

docs.title: Net load
docs.text:
Net load is demand minus wind and solar output. Scaling wind and solar models more installed capacity with the same weather:

\[N_t = L_t - k_w W_t - k_s S_t\] 
uv run openenergy netload data/time_series/time_series_60min_singleindex_filtered.csv
Year Renewable share Min net load (GW) 1 h ramp, p99 (GW) Price per GW of net load 2015 12.0% 11.3 7.3 £0.80/MWh 2017 16.5% 10.1 6.5 £1.23/MWh 2019 18.7% 6.7 7.1 £1.21/MWh 2020 (to Sep) 24.0% 3.1 7.1 £1.13/MWh

Each extra GW of net load raised the GB day-ahead price by about £1/MWh. Ramps are 99th percentiles of absolute changes, so a single bad reading cannot set them.

Load data quality

ENTSO-E's GB actual load has telemetry glitches, such as hours at 511 MW against real demand of 15 GW or more. load_system removes load readings that deviate from their 5-hour median by more than 25% of the 99th percentile, or fall below half their 7-day median (133 of 50,394 hours), and reports the count. Wind and solar are unchanged. The load is total demand, so subtracting solar does not double count it.

docs.title: Surplus as renewables grow
docs.text:
Surplus is renewable output the system cannot use: how far net load falls below a must-run floor \(F\) of inflexible generation, \(U_t = \max(0, F - N_t)\). examples/renewables_scaling.py scales 2019 wind and solar with an 8 GW floor:

Scale Renewable share Min net load (GW) 1 h ramp, p99 (GW) Surplus (TWh) Share of renewable output ×1 18.7% 6.7 7.0 0.00 0.0% ×2 37.4% −3.8 10.0 1.61 1.5% ×3 56.1% −20.2 14.1 14.39 8.6% ×4 74.8% −36.6 18.3 43.34 19.5%

Surplus grows much faster than capacity: doubling from ×2 to ×4 multiplies it by 27, and ramps steepen as renewables set more of the shape of net load.

docs.title: Storage to absorb surplus
docs.text:
A storage fleet charges from surplus and releases as soon as net load is back above the floor, never creating new surplus:

uv run openenergy storage data/time_series/time_series_60min_singleindex_filtered.csv \
  --scale-wind 3 --scale-solar 3 --must-run 8000 --power 2000,5000,10000 --hours 4,8,24

For 2019 with renewables ×3:

Power 4 h 8 h 24 h 2 GW 12.6% 17.5% 23.1% 5 GW 25.7% 35.7% 48.0% 10 GW 39.8% 54.4% 73.2%

Returns diminish with both power and duration, and duration matters: much of the surplus arrives in multi-day windy spells that short-duration storage cannot hold.

docs.title: Sizing a site
docs.text:
openenergy sweep runs any scenario over a grid of settings:

uv run openenergy sweep examples/gb-2019-naive.yaml \
  --set battery.energy_mwh=1,2,4 --set dispatch.degradation_cost=0,5,15

For a 1 MW battery in GB 2019 without a degradation cost, revenue per MW-year rises from £8.5k (1 h) to £15.8k (2 h) and £24.3k (4 h), so each extra hour earns less. A £15/MWh degradation cost exceeds most daily spreads and all but stops arbitrage.

docs.title: Emissions
docs.text:
With carbon intensity \(e_t\) in gCO2/kWh, a battery or site's net emissions are \(-\sum_t e_t\, x_t\, \Delta t / 1000\) tCO2 for net export \(x_t\): exports displace grid generation and imports add to it. Negative means net emissions avoided.

carbon.price_per_t steers dispatch by adding \(\lambda \hat e_t / 1000\) to the planning price. For the GB 2019 battery (examples/gb-2019-carbon.yaml at £50/t):

Carbon price Revenue Net emissions £0/t £13,447 −19.4 tCO2 £50/t £13,291 −21.2 tCO2 £200/t £12,616 −23.3 tCO2

Even without a carbon price, price arbitrage avoids emissions, because GB prices and carbon intensity move together (correlation 0.62). Each further tonne costs more: about £89 per tonne at £50/t and £212 at £200/t.

Average, not marginal

These use NESO's average grid intensity. Storage changes the marginal plant, whose emissions can differ, so results show direction and rough scale, not causal impact.

Why not NESO's forecast?

NESO's archived forecast is the last forecast issued before each half-hour, not the one available the day before. Planning on it at noon the day before raised the battery's revenue as the carbon price rose, which only leaked information can do. By default dispatch plans on the same hour's actual intensity a week earlier, cut off at the decision time like prices; planning: actual is an explicit upper bound.

docs.title: Web app
docs.text:
The web app is a simulator of Britain's grid with a battery trading on it, and values a battery on any GB day or year or on a NESO FES pathway's modelled prices. It answers in plain sentences and keeps the charts, assumptions and sources one click away. The pages are a React and TypeScript front end (web/); the year-long results come from a FastAPI JSON API (openenergy.app), and the simulator, Play and 2035 run in the browser. It runs at open-energy-eight.vercel.app, or locally:

uv sync                        # the app dependency group (FastAPI, plotly, uvicorn) is a default
npm --prefix web ci            # Node 22 or later
npm --prefix web run build     # writes web/dist, which the API serves
uv run uvicorn openenergy.app:app

Then open http://127.0.0.1:8000/. The app reads the repository's data/ folder (or $OPENENERGY_DATA) and the built pages from web/dist (or $OPENENERGY_WEB), so run it from a clone; pip install openenergy[app] installs the API and its dependencies only. To work on the pages, run the API as above and npm --prefix web run dev (Vite on port 5173, passing API calls to port 8000).

docs.title: In the browser
docs.text:
Page What it does / Simulator. Britain's grid hour by hour from 2019 to October 2026: generation by fuel flowing into the GB node, the day-ahead price, demand, carbon intensity and the wind share, with a battery charging and discharging on a plan the optimiser makes in the browser. Play at 1, 4 or 24 hours a second, step with ←/→ (shift for a day, space to play), or click a day on the year strip, coloured by each day's price spread. The side panel sets power, duration, efficiency and wear cost and the forecast the battery plans with; it shows the day's revenue for perfect foresight, OpenEnergy's forecast and last week's prices, and the whole year for all three, solved in the background a month at a time, with "best day" and "the forecast's worst miss". Notes appear on negative prices and price spikes. The address holds the day, hour and battery (/?day=2025-01-20&hour=16&mw=1&h=2&eff=95&wear=5&plan=fundamentals) /play Play: beat the battery. Tap or drag across the hours to plan a day from OpenEnergy's forecast; the battery (1 MW / 2 MWh, lossless, £5/MWh wear) starts and must end half full, as the optimiser's does. Run the day to see actual prices draw in and your cash against the optimiser on the same forecast and against perfect foresight; show the optimiser's plan to compare. The same day for everyone each day, and any day by link (/play?d=2024-03-12) /2035 The storage saturation study: pick a pathway and slide the battery fleet to see what one more battery earns, how hard the fleet works and how much firm capacity is still needed (/2035?pathway=Falling+Behind&fleet=2) /fleet Real batteries. What GB's grid batteries did each year from 2021, from Elexon's metered data: the fleet's estimated revenue next to the optimiser's, the fleet's average day against the day-ahead price, and every unit with its estimated total, metered energy at the day-ahead price and Balancing Mechanism cashflow per MW-year, by zone (/fleet?year=2025; Real batteries). The simulator also shows the real fleet's metered output each hour /research The pages below, for whole years, pathways and downloads /embed/arbitrage Draggable prices with the optimal plan, for the docs (Concepts)

?embed=1 shows the simulator or 2035 without the header, for embedding (as on Findings). The 6.0 addresses /lab and /replay open the simulator with their day and battery.

Revenue in these pages is after wear: what the plan earns at actual prices less the wear cost on every MWh moved, the quantity the optimiser maximises, so no plan beats perfect foresight. (The year results from the API below report revenue before wear, as the Python backtest does.)

These pages read static files (web/public/data/, written by scripts/build_app_data.py and served at /data/<file>): hourly prices and the fundamentals forecast for each year, the generation mix and carbon intensity, and the saturation study, each with its attribution. The optimiser is the same daily mixed-integer programme as openenergy.dispatch.optimise_dispatch, built in TypeScript (web/src/engine/) and solved by HiGHS compiled to WebAssembly (MIT, about 3.5 MB, loaded on first use). npm test checks it against the Python backtest on a month of 2025 for all three forecasts, day by day (engine-parity.json).

docs.title: From the API
docs.text:
Page What it does /run Form: historic GB year (2017–2025, Ember prices) or a FES pathway in 2030 or 2035; power (MW) and duration (0.5–8 hours); forecast (last week's prices, OpenEnergy's forecast from 2019, or perfect foresight); frequency response (none, Dynamic Containment, or Containment and Moderation; historic years from 2022) /result The answer: one sentence (revenue for your MW, share of perfect foresight, cycles a day), key numbers, cumulative and monthly revenue charts, what the result assumes, sources, and links to download it. At once for 1, 2 and 4 hour batteries; otherwise a progress counter while it runs /explore Battery value by GB year (2017–2025) and by FES pathway (2030, 2035) for one duration, forecast and response option, as bar charts and tables; click a bar to open its result /compare Up to three results side by side (table, revenue through the year, and each answer); the page address holds the comparison, so it can be shared, e.g. /compare?item=gb-2019&item=gb-2022&item=falling_behind_2030 /scenarios Each FES pathway's modelled results on 2025's weather next to NESO's own figures /download/daily.csv Daily revenue and perfect-foresight revenue for your MW, with the data credit on the first line /download/scenario.yaml The scenario that reproduces the result with openenergy run (or openenergy system run for a FES pathway) from the repository folder /battery The full hourly report of openenergy report (runs the backtest now) /health Status and version

Page addresses and their query parameters are the same as before v5.0 (the form moved from / to /run in v6.0), so shared results keep working. Every input and key number has a "?" next to it that explains it in a sentence (hover, tab to it, or tap). The battery uses 95% efficiency each way and a £5/MWh wear cost. Light and dark themes follow the system setting, and the button in the header switches them. On Vercel a run took 18 seconds for GB 2024, 14 seconds for a FES pathway and 44 seconds with Dynamic Containment (measured 14 October 2026). Pathway prices are precomputed in data/scenarios/ by scripts/build_scenario_prices.py (see Forward scenarios), so the app does not need PyPSA. Inputs are bounded query parameters, and error messages are fixed texts, never exception details.

docs.title: JSON API
docs.text:
The front end uses only this API, so anything it shows can be fetched directly:

Endpoint Returns /api/options Years, pathways, limits, forecast and service names, and the "?" explanations /api/result One battery: request, per-MW summary, daily revenue, and the answer, assumptions and sources for power_mw /api/explore Per-MW summaries by GB year (for services) and by FES pathway, for hours 1, 2 or 4 and forecast /api/compare Up to three results named by item (e.g. gb-2022-dc, falling_behind_2030), and every option /api/scenarios The FES pathway table with its note and attribution

/api/result takes source, year (history), pathway and target (scenario), hours, forecast, services and power_mw. Results are per MW, because revenue scales with power at a fixed duration:

{
  "key": "gb-2024-2h-naive_last_week-none",
  "label": "2 h battery, GB 2024",
  "precomputed": true,
  "request": {"source": "history", "year": 2024, "hours": 2.0, "prices": "gb-2024", "...": "..."},
  "summary": {"days": 366, "revenue_per_mw_year": 29048.5, "perfect_per_mw_year": 39304.0,
              "capture_ratio": 0.739, "cycles_per_day": 1.57, "captured_spread": 26.73,
              "forecast_mae": 19.54, "response_share": 0.0},
  "daily": {"date": ["2024-01-01", "..."], "revenue": [111.27, "..."],
            "benchmark_revenue": [241.64, "..."]},
  "text": {"power_mw": 1.0, "answer": "A 1 MW, 2-hour battery trading ...",
           "assumptions": ["..."], "sources": "..."}
}

1, 2 and 4 hour batteries on every year, forecast, response option and FES pathway are precomputed in data/app/ by scripts/build_app_results.py and return at once; other durations run live. A request that cannot run (for example frequency response before 2022) returns status 400 with an error message.

The front end's TypeScript types are generated from the API's OpenAPI schema: uv run python scripts/export_openapi.py writes web/src/api/openapi.json, and npm --prefix web run api-types turns it into web/src/api/schema.d.ts. CI fails if either is out of date.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text: uv run pytest tests/test_app.py checks the API; in web/, npm test runs the unit tests (Vitest) and npm run e2e runs the pages in Chromium against the real API (Playwright, after npm run build).

docs.title: Vercel
docs.text: The repository deploys to Vercel as one Python function. vercel.json builds the front end first (npm --prefix web ci && npm --prefix web run build); app.py at the root imports openenergy.app:app, which serves the API and the built pages. Vercel installs the project with uv, including the app dependency group (default groups other than dev); vercel.json gives the function up to 120 seconds and leaves out tests, docs, scripts, the front end's sources and data files the app does not read.
